Markedly elevated DHEA-S (> 700 µg/dL) indicates autonomous adrenal androgen production
Abdominal CT or MRI to visualize adrenal mass (adenoma vs adrenocortical carcinoma)
Complete hormonal workup: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, plasma ACTH
**Functional adrenal neoplasm present:** surgical adrenalectomy after medical optimization

triggers.text: increased hair growth over the face, chest, and lower abdomen
coarse hair over the upper lip, chin, and abdomen
serum dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate concentration is 75 µg/mL
overnight dexamethasone suppression test shows no suppression of cortisol

c-im-05-q045.boardCall: Severe hypercalcemia (15.2) + elevated PTH (800) + polyuria + dehydration -> Hypercalcemia-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
c-im-05-q045.hinge: Severe hypercalcemia impairs renal collecting duct ADH responsiveness via aquaporin-2 downregulation, causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
c-im-05-q045.trap: Excess thirst and polyuria suggest central DI or diabetes mellitus, but calcium of 15.2 blocks renal response to ADH.

A.clue: Drug-induced interstitial inflammation with eosinophiluria and rash
A.fit: Not here: no offending medications, primary hyperparathyroidism with severe hypercalcemia
A.tempting: acute renal dysfunction and urinary frequency in hospitalized patient

B.clue: Deficient hypothalamic synthesis or neurohypophyseal secretion of ADH
B.fit: Not here: pituitary produces ADH; collecting ducts are refractory
B.tempting: polyuria and polydipsia are classic features of diabetes insipidus

C.clue: Recurrent bacterial renal parenchymal infection with scarred calyces
C.fit: Not here: acute severe hypercalcemia, no pyuria or flank pain
C.tempting: urinary symptoms in a patient with chronic kidney disease

D.clue: Hyperglycemia exceeding renal threshold causing osmotic diuresis
D.fit: Not here: polyuria caused by hypercalcemia, not diabetic glycosuria
D.tempting: increased thirst and urinary frequency mimic osmotic diuresis

E.clue: Long-standing arteriolar nephrosclerosis causing chronic renal impairment
E.fit: Not here: acute 3-week lethargy and severe hypercalcemia 15.2
E.tempting: elevated blood pressure of 150/70 mm Hg

F.clue: Collecting duct resistance to ADH via aquaporin downregulation
F.fit: Here: calcium 15.2, polyuria, volume depletion, dry mucous membranes

nodes.text: Severe hypercalcemia (calcium > 14 mg/dL) + polyuria: assess for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
High calcium activates calcium-sensing receptors, downregulating aquaporin-2 water channels and inducing ADH resistance
Immediate aggressive intravenous 0.9% saline hydration to restore intravascular volume and enhance calciuresis
Add subcutaneous calcitonin for rapid calcium reduction + intravenous bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid)
**Refractory hypercalcemic crisis or oliguric renal failure:** perform urgent hemodialysis
Primary hyperparathyroidism confirmed (elevated PTH): elective parathyroidectomy after stabilization

triggers.text: increasing fatigue, constipation, urinary frequency, and increased thirst

c-im-05-q046.boardCall: African American woman + lung nodules + hypercalcemia + suppressed PTH + normal PTHrP -> Pulmonary sarcoidosis -> Systemic glucocorticoids
c-im-05-q046.hinge: Suppressed PTH and normal PTHrP with lung nodules and hypercalcemia point to 1-alpha-hydroxylase production in sarcoidosis, treated with glucocorticoids.
c-im-05-q046.trap: Hypercalcemia tempts parathyroidectomy, but suppressed PTH of 7 pg/mL excludes primary hyperparathyroidism.

A.clue: Exogenous active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3
A.fit: Not here: worsens hypercalcemia driven by excess endogenous calcitriol
A.tempting: vitamin D metabolite used in calcium metabolic disorders

B.clue: Anticonvulsant elevating brain GABA levels
B.fit: Not here: no seizure disorder or psychiatric mania
B.tempting: oral prescription pharmacotherapy unrelated to calcium homeostasis

C.clue: Inhibits osteoclastic bone resorption in malignancy-associated hypercalcemia
C.fit: Not here: second-line agent, nephrotoxic, does not treat sarcoidosis
C.tempting: pharmacotherapy used for malignancy-related hypercalcemia

D.clue: Inhibits 1-alpha-hydroxylase expression in activated macrophages
D.fit: Here: lung nodules, hypercalcemia 11.8, low PTH 7 pg/mL

E.clue: RNA synthesis inhibitor and cytotoxic antibiotic
E.fit: Not here: severe hepatotoxicity and thrombocytopenia, obsolete
E.tempting: historical cytoreductive option for refractory hypercalcemia

F.clue: Extracorporeal clearance of solutes and divalent cations
F.fit: Not here: calcium 11.8 mg/dL is mild-to-moderate, no renal failure
F.tempting: modality for severe refractory life-threatening hypercalcemia

G.clue: Surgical excision of hyperfunctioning parathyroid adenoma
G.fit: Not here: PTH is appropriately suppressed at 7 pg/mL
G.tempting: surgical standard of care for primary hyperparathyroidism

nodes.text: Hypercalcemia + low intact PTH (< 10 pg/mL) + normal PTHrP: measure 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Elevated 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D caused by macrophage 1-alpha-hydroxylase in sarcoid granulomas
High-resolution chest CT + bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas
Initiate systemic glucocorticoid therapy (oral prednisone) to inhibit granulomatous calcitriol synthesis
**Severe symptomatic hypercalcemia:** administer intravenous isotonic saline + subcutaneous calcitonin
Advise avoidance of direct sun exposure and dietary calcium and vitamin D supplements

triggers.text: several nodules throughout both lung fields

c-im-05-q047.boardCall: Hot summer day + core temp 40 C (104 F) + altered mental status + dry skin + multiorgan dysfunction -> Non-exertional (classic) heat stroke
c-im-05-q047.hinge: Core body temperature > 40 C with altered mental status following environmental heat exposure defines classic non-exertional heat stroke.
c-im-05-q047.trap: Alcoholism and tremor tempt delirium tremens or Wernicke encephalopathy, but hyperthermia of 40 C marks heat stroke.

A.clue: Autonomic hyperactivity, tremor, and delirium following alcohol cessation
A.fit: Not here: temperature 40 C, obtundation after heat wave
A.tempting: history of chronic alcoholism and tachycardia

B.clue: Thermoregulatory failure with hyperthermia > 40 C
B.fit: Here: temperature 40 C, obtundation, hot apartment, multiorgan injury

C.clue: Dopamine antagonist reaction with lead-pipe muscle rigidity
C.fit: Not here: no neuroleptic medications, no severe muscle rigidity
C.tempting: hyperthermia, altered mental status, and elevated creatine kinase

D.clue: Aneurysmal subarachnoid extravasation with thunderclap headache and meningismus
D.fit: Not here: CT head normal, supple neck, hyperthermia 40 C
D.tempting: obtunded elderly patient found down with altered consciousness

E.clue: Thyrotoxic crisis with tachycardia, agitation, and high fever
E.fit: Not here: dry warm skin in hot apartment, classic environmental exposure
E.tempting: hyperthermia, tachycardia, and altered mental status

F.clue: Thiamine deficiency triad of encephalopathy, oculomotor dysfunction, ataxia
F.fit: Not here: temperature 40 C, normal ocular movements, multiorgan failure
F.tempting: history of chronic alcoholism presenting with obtundation

nodes.text: Core body temperature > 40°C (104°F) + altered mental status after heat exposure: emergency heat stroke
Initiate immediate evaporative and convective cooling (mist water spray + large fans) to lower temperature
**Shivering during cooling:** administer intravenous benzodiazepines (lorazepam) to prevent metabolic heat generation
Target core temperature 38.3-38.9°C; cease active cooling to prevent hypothermic overshoot
Resuscitate with intravenous isotonic crystalloid fluids for dehydration and renal hypoperfusion
Monitor and manage complications: rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, hepatic necrosis, and coagulopathy

triggers.text: unconscious in his apartment on a hot summer day
obtunded but is responsive to painful stimuli
warm, dry skin and dry mucous membranes
CT scan of the head show no abnormalities

c-im-05-q048.boardCall: Alcohol use disorder + postural hand tremor + hyperreflexia + hypocalcemia -> Hypomagnesemia
c-im-05-q048.hinge: Alcoholism with neuromuscular excitability (tremor, hyperreflexia) and concurrent hypocalcemia characteristically indicates underlying hypomagnesemia.
c-im-05-q048.trap: Hypokalemia is common in alcoholics, but neuromuscular hyperreflexia paired with hypocalcemia specifically points to magnesium deficiency.

A.clue: Chloride depletion typically secondary to vomiting or diuretics
A.fit: Not here: no vomiting or diuretic use, lacks neuromuscular hyperexcitability
A.tempting: electrolyte disturbance that can accompany metabolic alkalosis

B.clue: Potassium deficit causing muscular weakness, cramps, and dysrhythmias
B.fit: Not here: causes hyporeflexia and weakness, not hyperreflexia
B.tempting: frequently seen in chronic alcoholism due to poor intake

C.clue: Magnesium deficiency inducing neuromuscular hyperexcitability and PTH resistance
C.fit: Here: alcoholism, postural tremor, hyperreflexia, concurrent low calcium

D.clue: Hypoosmolar state causing cerebral edema and lethargy
D.fit: Not here: produces confusion or seizures, not isolated hyperreflexia
D.tempting: beer potomania and chronic malnutrition cause hyponatremia

E.clue: Phosphate depletion leading to proximal muscle weakness
E.fit: Not here: causes muscle weakness rather than brisk hyperreflexia
E.tempting: common in refeeding syndrome and severe chronic alcoholism

nodes.text: Tremor + hyperreflexia + refractory hypocalcemia in alcoholism: measure serum magnesium concentration
Magnesium depletion impairs parathyroid hormone release and creates peripheral PTH organ resistance
Replete magnesium with intravenous magnesium sulfate or oral magnesium oxide
**Refractory hypocalcemia or hypokalemia:** will not correct until serum magnesium is normalized
Provide oral thiamine, folate, and multivitamin supplementation before carbohydrate administration
Assess and treat underlying alcohol withdrawal syndrome with symptom-triggered benzodiazepines

triggers.text: hyperreflexia and a tremor in both hands
transferred from the hospital to a drug rehabilitation facility

c-im-05-q049.boardCall: Incapacitated patient + valid clear advance directive + family requests aggressive care -> Honor and follow the advance directive
c-im-05-q049.hinge: A patient's clear, valid advance directive supersedes conflicting surrogate requests when the patient lacks decision-making capacity.
c-im-05-q049.trap: Conflicting family requests tempt ethics or legal consultation, but a valid directive with prior competent refusal is legally binding.

A.clue: Hospital legal counsel consultation for unresolvable statutory dilemmas
A.fit: Not here: clear valid advance directive does not require legal consultation
A.tempting: sibling dispute creates potential threat of hospital litigation

B.clue: Multidisciplinary institutional advisory review for ethical disputes
B.fit: Not here: patient's documented advance wishes are unambiguous and confirmed
B.tempting: family conflict over end-of-life care often prompts ethics consultation

C.clue: Honors patient's autonomous prior documented healthcare decisions
C.fit: Here: valid advance directive refusing lifesaving measures, verbal confirmation

D.clue: Initiates temporary invasive life support during family disagreement
D.fit: Not here: directly violates patient's autonomous documented refusal of care
D.tempting: maintains life while resolving family discord regarding treatment goals

E.clue: Intubation, mechanical ventilation, and aggressive intensive care
E.fit: Not here: patient and oncologist explicitly discontinued treatment 9 months ago
E.tempting: both adult siblings requested switching to aggressive treatment

nodes.text: Incapacitated patient facing end-of-life decisions: determine if valid advance directive or healthcare proxy exists
Follow the advance directive refusing life-prolonging intervention despite surrogate or family objections
**Surrogate attempts to override valid directive:** explain that patient's autonomous written wishes supersede surrogate preferences
**Ambiguous or absent advance directive:** surrogate makes substituted judgment based on patient's known values
Transition focus to comfort-oriented palliative care and aggressive symptom management (opioids, hydration)
Provide emotional support and grief counseling for family members at bedside

triggers.text: advance directive indicating that he does not want lifesaving treatment
son has stated that his father recently confirmed these wishes verbally
both siblings now request that the physician switch to an aggressive treatment plan
Nine months ago, he and his oncologist agreed to discontinue treatment

c-im-05-q050.boardCall: Hyperthyroidism (TSH < 0.3) + single discrete 2-cm thyroid nodule -> Toxic (hyperfunctioning) thyroid adenoma
c-im-05-q050.hinge: Suppressed TSH with overt thyrotoxicosis and a solitary thyroid nodule defines a toxic thyroid adenoma.
c-im-05-q050.trap: Malignancy tempts solitary nodule, but thyroid carcinomas are nonfunctional cold nodules that do not suppress TSH.

A.clue: TSH-receptor autoantibodies causing diffuse symmetric thyroid hyperplasia
A.fit: Not here: solitary 2-cm nodule, lacks diffuse goiter or orbitopathy
A.tempting: young female with heat intolerance, weight loss, and low TSH

B.clue: Parafollicular C-cell neuroendocrine neoplasm secreting calcitonin
B.fit: Not here: cold nonfunctioning nodule, does not cause hyperthyroidism
B.tempting: discrete firm solitary thyroid nodule in a young woman

C.clue: Malignant follicular epithelial neoplasm with psammoma bodies
C.fit: Not here: nonfunctioning cold nodule, does not suppress TSH
C.tempting: solitary firm thyroid nodule raises concern for thyroid malignancy

D.clue: Invasive dense fibrosclerosis of thyroid and adjacent neck
D.fit: Not here: causes 'woody' fixed goiter and hypothyroidism, not hyperthyroidism
D.tempting: firm thyroid nodular mass on physical examination

E.clue: Autonomous hyperfunctioning monoclonal follicular adenoma
E.fit: Here: suppressed TSH < 0.3, solitary 2-cm nodule, hyperthyroidism

F.clue: Multiple autonomous hyperfunctioning nodules with patchy uptake
F.fit: Not here: solitary discrete nodule, not multiple palpable nodules
F.tempting: autonomous hyperthyroidism without Graves eye disease

nodes.text: Low TSH (< 0.4 µU/mL) + solitary thyroid nodule: radioactive iodine (RAI) uptake and scan
**Hot (hyperfunctioning) nodule:** toxic adenoma (focal high tracer uptake with suppressed background)
**Cold (nonfunctioning) nodule:** perform fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy for cytology
Control adrenergic symptoms with oral beta-blockers (propranolol or atenolol)
Definitive management: radioactive iodine ablation (I-131) or surgical thyroid lobectomy
Avoid fine-needle aspiration biopsy for hot nodules because malignancy is exceedingly rare

triggers.text: fatigue, heat intolerance, generalized anxiety, and intermittent palpitations
2-cm, discrete, firm nodule in the left lobe of the thyroid gland
serum thyroid-stimulating hormone concentration is less than 0.3 µU/mL

acid-base-disorders.name: Acid-base disorders
acid-base-disorders.scope: Metabolic acidosis (anion gap, non-anion gap), metabolic alkalosis (saline-responsive vs saline-resistant), respiratory acidosis, respiratory alkalosis, Winter formula, mixed disorders
acid-base-disorders.core: Identify the primary pH disturbance, test expected compensation, then investigate the anion gap or urine chloride to locate the cause.

rows.label: Definition
items: Acidemia: pH <7.35; alkalemia: >7.45; normal pH can hide opposing primary disorders
Metabolic: primary HCO3 change; respiratory: primary PaCO2 change

rows.label: Formula
items: ★ **AG = Na − (Cl + HCO3)**; usual normal ≈8–12, laboratory dependent
Hypoalbuminemia correction: add 2.5 to AG per 1 g/dL albumin below 4
★ **Winter: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 ±2**

rows.label: Interpret
items: HCO3 12 → expected PaCO2 26 ±2; measured 40 → additional respiratory acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis: expected PaCO2 ≈40 + 0.7 × (HCO3 − 24), ±5
Respiratory HCO3 change per 10 PaCO2: acidosis +1 acute/+4 chronic; alkalosis −2 acute/−4 chronic

rows.label: Use when
items: ★ Alkalosis: **urine Cl <20 mmol/L** → saline-responsive; ≥20 → diuretics/mineralocorticoids
ΔAG exceeds HCO3 fall → additional alkalosis; smaller ΔAG → additional non-gap acidosis

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ Compensation never overshoots; values outside expected range imply **mixed disorder**
Salicylates often cause respiratory alkalosis plus high-gap acidosis; near-normal pH is deceptive
Diarrhea/RTA: non-gap acidosis; renal failure: either gap pattern

acid-base-disorders.evidence: Established physiologic formulas; no guideline involved.

acute-kidney-injury.name: Acute kidney injury
acute-kidney-injury.core: Abrupt loss of renal filtration: separate impaired perfusion, parenchymal injury, and urinary obstruction before treating the cause.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Volume depletion, sepsis, heart failure, cirrhosis; baseline CKD increases vulnerability
NSAIDs constrict afferent arterioles; ACE inhibitors/ARBs reduce efferent tone during hypoperfusion
Aminoglycosides, pigment injury, prolonged ischemia → tubular damage; antibiotics/PPIs → interstitial inflammation

rows.label: Clues
items: Oliguria, edema, uremic nausea; urine output may remain normal
AIN: fever, rash, eosinophilia sometimes present; classic triad often absent
★ Pulmonary edema, severe hyperkalemia, encephalopathy, pericarditis → **urgent renal support**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced glomerular pressure, tubular epithelial injury, or backpressure → declining GFR

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ AKI: creatinine ↑≥0.3 mg/dL within 48 h, ≥1.5-fold within 7 days, or oliguria
Oliguria criterion: urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h; trend creatinine, electrolytes, fluid balance
★ **Urinalysis + microscopy**, medication review; bladder scan → renal ultrasound if obstruction possible
FeNa unreliable with diuretics, CKD, early obstruction; urine eosinophils neither sensitive nor specific
Unexplained persistent injury or suspected glomerulonephritis → nephrology, possible kidney biopsy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Severe hyperkalemia → **IV calcium**, insulin/dextrose; refractory electrolyte disturbance → dialysis
Hypovolemia → isotonic crystalloid; congestion → loop diuretic; avoid reflex fluids in overloaded patients
Stop culprit nephrotoxins; renal-dose drugs; AIN persisting after withdrawal → consider glucocorticoids
★ Obstruction → **catheter or ureteral decompression**; monitor postobstructive diuresis
Dialysis: refractory acidosis, hyperkalemia, intoxication, overload, symptomatic uremia; no isolated creatinine threshold

rows.label: Complications
items: Arrhythmias, acidosis, volume overload; subsequent CKD
Recovery diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte losses

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain perfusion during illness; review nephrotoxic combinations and monitor renal function

rows.label: Mimics
items: CKD: longstanding abnormalities, small echogenic kidneys, chronic anemia
Trimethoprim effect: creatinine rise without true GFR decline

acute-kidney-injury.evidence: Not checked online; established KDIGO diagnostic criteria and renal teaching.

adrenal-masses.name: Adrenal masses
adrenal-masses.scope: Adrenal incidentaloma, adrenocortical carcinoma, functional vs nonfunctional evaluation, pheochromocytoma, hyperaldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, hyperandrogenism (DHEA-S), adrenal CT imaging, adrenalectomy indications
adrenal-masses.core: An incidental adrenal lesion requires two decisions: malignant potential on imaging and clinically important hormone secretion.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Incidental detection increases with age; known extra-adrenal cancer raises metastatic risk
MEN2/VHL/NF1 predispose to pheochromocytoma; most incidental lesions are benign cortical adenomas

rows.label: Clues
items: Often asymptomatic; weight loss, flank pain, rapid growth, or mixed steroid excess suggest carcinoma
Episodic headache/palpitations/diaphoresis → catecholamines; proximal weakness/easy bruising → cortisol excess
Resistant hypertension/hypokalemia → aldosterone; rapid virilization → adrenal androgen secretion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cortical tumors may secrete cortisol, aldosterone, or androgens; medullary tumors secrete catecholamines
Autonomous cortisol suppresses ACTH and contralateral adrenal function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast adrenal CT** first; assess density, homogeneity, size, invasion; indeterminate → dedicated imaging
★ **1 mg overnight dexamethasone**: cortisol >1.8 µg/dL suggests autonomy; confirm ACTH independence
Plasma free or urinary fractionated metanephrines if lesion not clearly benign or pheochromocytoma symptoms
Hypertension/hypokalemia → aldosterone/renin ratio; suspected carcinoma or virilization → DHEA-S and steroid precursors
★ **Never biopsy before excluding pheochromocytoma**; biopsy rarely distinguishes adenoma from cortical carcinoma

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinically significant unilateral hormone excess → **adrenalectomy**; suspected carcinoma requires preoperative staging
Pheochromocytoma: alpha blockade and volume repletion before surgery; beta blockade only afterward if needed
Mild cortisol autonomy: individualize surgery by diabetes, hypertension, skeletal disease, and operative risk
Indeterminate unoperated lesion → repeat CT/MRI in 6–12 months; growth prompts reassessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Pheochromocytoma manipulation → hypertensive crisis; carcinoma → metastases
Postoperative adrenal insufficiency after cortisol-producing tumor removal → perioperative glucocorticoid coverage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Address cortisol-associated cardiometabolic and bone risk; genetic counseling for syndromic catecholamine tumors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Myelolipoma: macroscopic fat on CT
Adrenal metastasis: cancer history, often bilateral; biopsy only if management changes
Adrenal hemorrhage: acute pain, anticoagulation/trauma context, evolving imaging appearance

table.title: Imaging changes the answer
rows: Benign; no further imaging regardless of size

advance-directives-and-surrogates.name: Advance directives and surrogate decisions
advance-directives-and-surrogates.scope: Living will, DNR/DNI orders, health care proxy, substituted judgment, best interests, advance care planning
advance-directives-and-surrogates.core: Follow the capable patient's current wishes; when capacity is absent, use valid directives and authorized surrogate judgment.

rows.label: Principle
items: Autonomy persists after incapacity through documented preferences and legally authorized decision-makers
Substituted judgment: patient's known values; best interests: benefits/burdens when preferences unknown

rows.label: Do
items: ★ Confirm capacity, directive validity, clinical applicability, and designated **health care proxy**
★ Apply the patient's instructions over conflicting surrogate preferences
Discuss goals early; document resuscitation preferences and identify a surrogate before crisis

rows.label: Don't
items: ★ **DNR limits CPR**; do not automatically withhold antibiotics, analgesia, nutrition, or other treatment
Do not equate disagreement with the team or family with invalid decision-making

rows.label: Exceptions
items: Capable patient may revise prior instructions; current informed choices control
No directive/proxy → statutory surrogate hierarchy; emergency treatment while authority is clarified
Conflict or harmful surrogate decisions → ethics consultation; court review if unresolved

rows.label: Traps
items: ★ **DNI and DNR differ**; clarify acceptable ventilation and perioperative plans
Advance directive does not require terminal illness to appoint a proxy
Surrogate represents patient preferences rather than the surrogate's own beliefs

table.title: Documents and authority
rows: Durable health care power of attorney
Current medical order limiting specified intervention
Portable treatment orders for serious illness

advance-directives-and-surrogates.evidence: Not checked online; established ethics framework; document validity and surrogate hierarchy depend on jurisdiction.

airway-management.name: Airway management
airway-management.scope: Indications for endotracheal intubation (GCS <= 8, airway protection, respiratory failure), rapid sequence intubation, bag-valve-mask ventilation, difficult airway
airway-management.core: Secure the airway when oxygenation, ventilation, or protection fails; preparation and rescue oxygenation determine safety.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Facial/neck trauma, burns, angioedema, obesity, limited jaw opening or cervical mobility
Shock, severe hypoxemia, metabolic acidosis increase peri-intubation collapse risk

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **GCS ≤8**, absent protective reflexes, recurrent aspiration, apnea → assess need for definitive airway
Stridor, fatigue, rising CO₂, refractory hypoxemia, inability to handle secretions → impending failure
GCS alone imperfect: reversible intoxication without ventilation/protection failure may permit closely monitored observation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Upper-airway obstruction, depressed drive, or respiratory muscle failure prevents effective gas exchange
Induction/positive pressure reduces sympathetic tone and venous return, worsening hypotension

rows.label: Dx
items: Continuous pulse oximetry, ECG, BP; assess mouth opening, neck anatomy, aspiration risk
★ Confirm tracheal placement with **persistent waveform capnography**, then auscultation and chest radiograph for depth
Do not rely on chest movement, oxygen saturation, or auscultation alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Position, suction, **preoxygenate**; prepare BVM, supraglottic device, video laryngoscope, and surgical rescue
Two-person BVM with airway adjunct and oxygen; oral adjunct only without gag reflex
RSI: etomidate/ketamine + rocuronium/succinylcholine; provide immediate postintubation analgesia and sedation
★ Predicted difficult airway → awake intubation strategy; **cannot intubate/cannot oxygenate → cricothyrotomy**
Avoid succinylcholine: hyperkalemia, denervation, established major burns, neuromuscular disease, malignant hyperthermia risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Esophageal/right-mainstem intubation, aspiration, dental injury, hypoxemia, cardiac arrest
Positive-pressure ventilation → barotrauma; prolonged ventilation → pneumonia, laryngeal injury

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Optimize **hemodynamics before induction**, use attempt limits and explicit backup plan
Head-of-bed elevation, oral care, daily sedation/ventilator liberation assessment

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic hyperventilation: preserved oxygenation/protection, respiratory alkalosis
Compensatory Kussmaul breathing: metabolic acidosis; losing minute ventilation can cause abrupt deterioration

airway-management.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency airway principles.

ards.name: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
ards.scope: Berlin definition, PaO2/FiO2 ratio, noncardiogenic pulmonary edema (normal PCWP), increased capillary permeability, lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volume, PEEP), prone positioning
ards.core: Acute refractory hypoxemia and bilateral opacities after a major inflammatory insult, without hydrostatic edema explaining the respiratory failure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, major trauma, pancreatitis, near-drowning, massive transfusion

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid tachypnea, increased work of breathing, diffuse crackles; oxygen requirements escalate
Severe disease: cyanosis, exhaustion, altered mentation, hypotension, multiorgan dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ★ Diffuse alveolar-capillary injury → **increased permeability**, protein-rich edema, hyaline membranes
Surfactant loss and alveolar collapse → decreased compliance and intrapulmonary shunt

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Berlin: onset **within 1 week**, bilateral imaging opacities, respiratory failure not explained by cardiac overload
ABG and FiO2 quantify severity; classification requires PEEP or CPAP ≥5 cm H2O
Echocardiography if hydrostatic edema remains plausible; PCWP generally normal, but pulmonary artery catheter unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat precipitating cause; oxygen → intubation for severe respiratory distress or refractory hypoxemia
★ Ventilate at **6 mL/kg predicted body weight**; plateau pressure ≤30 cm H2O
★ Moderate/severe → higher **PEEP**; PaO2/FiO2 <150 despite support → prone >12 hours/day
After shock resolves → conservative fluid strategy; avoid prolonged high-pressure recruitment maneuvers
Consider corticosteroids; early severe dyssynchrony → neuromuscular blockade; refractory severe disease → VV-ECMO evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Ventilator-induced lung injury, pneumothorax, ventilator-associated pneumonia
Critical illness weakness, delirium, persistent exercise limitation; mortality often reflects underlying multiorgan failure

rows.label: Prevention
items: Aspiration precautions, infection prevention, prompt sepsis treatment; avoid unnecessary transfusions
Daily sedation assessment, spontaneous breathing trials when improving, venous thromboembolism prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiogenic edema: elevated filling pressures, LV dysfunction, improvement with decongestion
Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage: falling hemoglobin; progressively bloodier bronchoalveolar lavage
Pulmonary embolism: hypoxemia with relatively clear imaging; CT pulmonary angiography identifies thrombus

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Atopy, family history, allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ **No SABA-only treatment or LABA monotherapy**; current GINA differs from older intermittent-asthma teaching

rows.label: Mimics
items: Inducible laryngeal obstruction: inspiratory stridor, inspiratory flow-loop flattening
COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings

atrioventricular-block.name: Atrioventricular block
atrioventricular-block.scope: First-degree, second-degree Mobitz type I (Wenckebach), second-degree Mobitz type II, third-degree (complete) AV block, atropine, pacemaker indications
atrioventricular-block.core: Impaired atrial-to-ventricular conduction ranges from harmless delay to complete dissociation; symptoms and level of block determine urgency and pacing.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age-related conduction fibrosis, MI, beta blockers, verapamil/diltiazem, digoxin, hyperkalemia
Lyme carditis, infiltrative disease, myocarditis, cardiac surgery; high vagal tone causes benign nodal delay

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, exertional intolerance, presyncope/syncope; cannon A waves with AV dissociation
★ Hypotension, confusion, ischemic discomfort, acute heart failure → **symptomatic unstable bradycardia**
Wide QRS and slow escape suggest distal disease; narrow escape may still be dangerous

rows.label: Pathophys
items: AV-nodal block often responds to vagal withdrawal; His–Purkinje failure risks unpredictable progression and asystole

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **12-lead ECG** establishes conduction pattern; continuous monitoring for significant block
Review drugs, electrolytes, ischemia; targeted Lyme testing with exposure; echo for structural disease
2:1 block cannot be labeled Mobitz I versus II from ratio alone; assess QRS and localization

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable → airway/oxygen if needed, IV access, **atropine** while preparing pacing
★ Atropine ineffective or distal high-grade block → **transcutaneous pacing**, then temporary transvenous pacing
Epinephrine/dopamine infusion can bridge to pacing; confirm electrical and mechanical capture
Stop AV-nodal blockers and correct reversible cause; do not wait for atropine in deteriorating infranodal disease
Permanent pacing for acquired Mobitz II, high-grade, or complete block without reversible cause, even asymptomatic

rows.label: Complications
items: Adams–Stokes syncope, low-output failure, ventricular arrhythmia, sudden death
Pacemaker implantation → infection, pneumothorax, lead problems; prolonged RV pacing may impair LV function

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication review, ischemia/electrolyte treatment; asymptomatic first-degree or nodal Mobitz I usually observation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Blocked premature atrial beat: early hidden P wave, noncompensatory pause
Sinus arrest: absent P waves during pause
AV dissociation from VT: ventricular tachycardia drives rhythm

table.title: ECG distinction
rows: Progressive PR lengthening, then dropped QRS
Constant conducted PR, sudden dropped QRS

autoimmune-biliary-diseases.name: Autoimmune biliary diseases
autoimmune-biliary-diseases.scope: Primary sclerosing cholangitis, primary biliary cholangitis, bead-like strictures on MRCP, AMA, ursodeoxycholic acid
autoimmune-biliary-diseases.core: Chronic cholestasis with pruritus and fatigue suggests immune-mediated bile-duct disease; anatomy and serology distinguish the major types.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Coexisting autoimmune disease; family susceptibility
PSC strongly associated with ulcerative colitis; PBC usually middle-aged women

rows.label: Clues
items: Disproportionate ALP/GGT elevation; bilirubin may remain normal early
Excoriations, jaundice, hepatomegaly; xanthelasma and fat malabsorption with prolonged cholestasis
★ Fever, RUQ pain, new jaundice → **acute bacterial cholangitis**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic duct injury → impaired bile flow, progressive fibrosis and biliary cirrhosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Cholestatic labs → **RUQ ultrasound** first to exclude mechanical obstruction
PBC usually diagnosed with cholestasis plus disease-specific antibodies; biopsy if atypical/seronegative
PSC with normal cholangiogram and persistent suspicion → biopsy for small-duct disease
New dominant/relevant stricture → ERCP with sampling for cholangiocarcinoma; not routine diagnostic ERCP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Ursodeoxycholic acid** first-line PBC; inadequate response/intolerance → seladelpar or elafibranor
PSC: no established disease-modifying drug; avoid high-dose ursodeoxycholic acid
Bacterial cholangitis → antibiotics and biliary drainage; obstructive stricture → endoscopic intervention
Cholestyramine for itch; advanced decompensation or refractory symptoms → liver transplant
Obeticholic acid withdrawn in US 2025 → not a current second-line choice

rows.label: Complications
items: Portal hypertension, hepatic failure, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, osteoporosis
PSC → cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer, colorectal cancer with IBD

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Bone-density assessment, vitamin replacement when deficient; hepatitis A/B vaccination
PSC → colonoscopy for occult IBD and ongoing cancer surveillance; cirrhosis → HCC surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: discrete obstructing stone; IgG4 cholangitis: pancreatic disease, steroid responsiveness
Drug cholestasis: temporal drug exposure without characteristic chronic duct findings

chronic-kidney-disease.name: Chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal disease
chronic-kidney-disease.scope: CKD progression, anemia of CKD (erythropoietin deficiency), mineral and bone disorder, uremic complications, volume overload, indications for emergent dialysis (AEIOU), vascular access
chronic-kidney-disease.core: Persistent kidney injury or reduced filtration causes progressive cardiovascular, metabolic and uremic complications; dialysis follows clinical indications rather than creatinine alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diabetes, hypertension, glomerular disease, obstruction, recurrent AKI, inherited cystic disease
NSAIDs, smoking and uncontrolled proteinuria accelerate progression

rows.label: Clues
items: Early disease often asymptomatic; advanced disease → fatigue, pruritus, anorexia, edema
Uremia: confusion, pericardial friction rub, nausea or bleeding despite normal platelet count
Labs: normocytic anemia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, ↑phosphate, low/normal calcium

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nephron loss → hyperfiltration in remaining nephrons, proteinuria and fibrosis
↓Erythropoietin causes anemia; phosphate retention/↓calcitriol → secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **eGFR <60** or kidney-damage markers for **≥3 months** establishes CKD
Urine albumin/creatinine ratio, urinalysis, creatinine trend; ultrasound for size/obstruction
Stage by GFR and albuminuria; small echogenic kidneys support chronicity but are not universal
Monitor CBC, ferritin/TSAT, K, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate and PTH

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Albuminuric CKD → **ACE inhibitor/ARB**; monitor creatinine/K; never combine both
SGLT2 inhibitor for T2DM or qualifying albuminuric CKD/HF, generally starting eGFR ≥20
Overload → salt restriction, furosemide; high phosphate → sevelamer; selected severe hyperparathyroidism → calcitriol
Iron repletion before ESA for selected persistent anemia; correct clinically significant metabolic acidosis
★ **Dialysis (AEIOU)**: refractory acidosis/hyperkalemia/overload, dialyzable toxins, uremic complications

rows.label: Complications
items: Cardiovascular death, fractures, severe hyperkalemic arrhythmia, malnutrition
Dialysis access infection/thrombosis; rapid urea reduction → dialysis disequilibrium

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Preserve arm veins; plan **AV fistula** before hemodialysis; temporary catheter for emergencies; early transplant referral
BP/glycemic control, avoid nephrotoxins, renal drug adjustment; hepatitis B vaccination before dialysis

rows.label: Mimics
items: AKI: acute creatinine change; may complicate established CKD
Prerenal azotemia: reversible perfusion deficit without persistent structural injury

chronic-venous-insufficiency.name: Chronic venous insufficiency
chronic-venous-insufficiency.scope: Varicose veins, stasis dermatitis, venous stasis ulcers, superficial thrombophlebitis, post-thrombotic syndrome
chronic-venous-insufficiency.core: Venous hypertension produces dependent edema, hemosiderin pigmentation, and shallow medial ankle ulcers that improve with elevation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior DVT, obesity, pregnancy, prolonged standing, older age, family history
Reduced calf-muscle pumping from immobility; previous leg trauma or venous surgery

rows.label: Clues
items: Aching/heaviness worsened by standing; varicosities, pitting swelling, preserved pedal pulses
Eczematous itching, lipodermatosclerosis, inverted champagne-bottle leg contour
★ **Irregular, exudative gaiter-region wound**; bilateral erythema without systemic illness favors stasis dermatitis
Superficial thrombophlebitis: focal erythema over a tender palpable venous cord

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Valve failure or outflow obstruction → reflux, capillary leakage, chronic inflammation
Post-thrombotic syndrome: residual obstruction and valvular injury following DVT

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous duplex ultrasound** evaluates reflux and obstruction; clinical examination often establishes diagnosis
★ **Ankle-brachial index before compression** when PAD suspected; <0.5 → avoid sustained compression
Nonhealing or atypical ulcer → biopsy for malignancy; sudden unilateral worsening → evaluate acute DVT
New superficial cord → assess clot length, proximity to deep junction, associated DVT

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Adequate arterial inflow → **compression bandaging/stockings + leg elevation**; walking activates calf pump
Ulcers: saline cleansing, moist absorbent dressings, debridement when needed
Stasis dermatitis: emollients plus short-course topical corticosteroid on intact inflamed skin
Symptomatic superficial reflux → endovenous ablation; moderate arterial disease → specialist-guided reduced compression
No antibiotics for colonization alone; cellulitis → systemic antibiotics; no routine diuretics without volume overload

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent ulceration, cellulitis, contact dermatitis; superficial clot can extend into deep veins
Chronic wounds rarely undergo squamous malignant transformation; new growth or bleeding warrants biopsy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Weight reduction, regular mobility, avoid prolonged dependent posture
Long-term compression after ulcer healing reduces recurrence; moisturize skin and treat venous reflux

rows.label: Mimics
items: Arterial ulcer: painful punched-out toes/lateral ankle, cool foot, weak pulses
Neuropathic ulcer: plantar pressure points, sensory loss, callus
Lymphedema: dorsal foot/toe swelling, later nonpitting thickened skin

table.title: Superficial thrombosis treatment
rows: Short distal segment, no high-risk features
≥5 cm long, >3 cm from deep junction

chronic-venous-insufficiency.evidence: Thrombosis checked 2026-10-30: [SVS/AVF/AVLS 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11523430/); wound care established teaching.

contact-dermatitis.name: Contact dermatitis
contact-dermatitis.scope: Allergic contact dermatitis (poison ivy/urushiol, nickel, neomycin, type IV hypersensitivity), irritant contact dermatitis, patch testing, topical corticosteroids, allergen avoidance
contact-dermatitis.core: Pruritic eczema confined to an exposure pattern; delayed allergy or direct chemical injury, sometimes spreading beyond contact sites.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Allergens: urushiol, nickel jewelry, fragrances, latex additives, neomycin, occupational chemicals
Irritants: repeated handwashing, detergents, solvents, prolonged wet work; atopic skin increases susceptibility

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Linear vesicles** after outdoor exposure; geometric plaques under jewelry, adhesive, or topical products
Acute: erythema, edema, weeping; chronic: fissuring, scaling, lichenification
Irritant disease often burns or stings; allergic disease usually itches
Extensive blistering, facial swelling, genital involvement → assess severity and secondary infection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allergic: sensitized T cells mediate **type IV hypersensitivity**; symptoms 24–72 hours after re-exposure
Irritant: direct epidermal barrier damage; no prior sensitization required

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical exposure history and distribution first; review work, hobbies, cosmetics, and new skin products
Persistent or unclear allergic disease → **patch testing**, read after delayed intervals
Skin-prick testing and serum IgE do not diagnose delayed contact allergy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Remove exposure → emollients and **topical corticosteroids**; choose potency by body site
Face, groin, folds: low-potency hydrocortisone; thick extremity plaques: triamcinolone
★ Poison ivy **>20% BSA** or severe face/genital disease → oral prednisone taper **2–3 weeks**
Cool wet compresses for oozing; antibiotics only for bacterial superinfection

rows.label: Complications
items: Excoriation → impetigo; persistent exposure → chronic hand eczema and work disability
Prolonged potent topical steroids → skin atrophy, striae; systemic steroids → hyperglycemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Protective gloves and barrier care; fragrance-free products; avoid the identified allergen
Wash urushiol promptly from skin, clothing, and tools; blister fluid does not spread dermatitis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Atopic dermatitis: chronic flexural eczema, personal or family atopy
Tinea: advancing annular scaly border; KOH reveals hyphae
Scabies: nocturnal itch, finger-web burrows, affected close contacts

contact-dermatitis.evidence: Not checked online; established dermatology teaching.

dyslipidemia.name: Dyslipidemia
dyslipidemia.scope: Lipid screening guidelines, ASCVD risk calculation, statin therapy indications, monitoring response to diet and pharmacotherapy
dyslipidemia.core: Excess atherogenic lipoproteins drive ASCVD; treatment intensity follows established disease, severe LDL elevation, diabetes, and estimated absolute cardiovascular risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Familial disorders, saturated-fat intake, obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis
Premature ASCVD family history, CKD, smoking, inflammatory disease increase treatment benefit

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; tendon xanthomas/early corneal arcus suggest familial hypercholesterolemia
Severe triglyceride elevation: eruptive xanthomas, pancreatitis; low HDL alone is not a drug target

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retained apoB-containing particles → arterial inflammation and plaque formation
Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → hepatic LDL-receptor upregulation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Lipid panel from age 19, at least every 5 years**; earlier/more often with risk
Nonfasting panel acceptable; markedly high triglycerides → fasting repeat/secondary-cause evaluation; Lp(a) once/lifetime
★ **PREVENT-ASCVD**, ages 30–79, LDL 70–189 without ASCVD: replaces pooled-cohort equations in 2026 guidance
Uncertain statin decision → coronary calcium; zero insufficient for deferral with diabetes, smoking, strong premature history

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Clinical ASCVD or **LDL ≥190 mg/dL → high-intensity statin**, no risk calculation required
★ Diabetes age 40–75 → **at least moderate-intensity statin**; multiple risk factors favor high intensity
Above LDL target despite maximal statin → ezetimibe; consider PCSK9 inhibitor or bempedoic acid
Severe triglycerides ≥500 → address causes, diet, consider fenofibrate/prescription omega-3 to reduce pancreatitis risk

rows.label: Complications
items: MI, stroke, peripheral arterial disease; statins → myalgias, rare rhabdomyolysis, small diabetes-risk increase
Baseline ALT; CK only with symptoms/risk; most lipid-lowering drugs deferred during conception/pregnancy/lactation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Mediterranean-style diet, replace saturated fats, exercise, weight reduction, smoking cessation
★ Recheck lipids **4–12 weeks after starting/changing drugs**, then every 6–12 months; assess adherence
High intensity lowers LDL ≥50%: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hypothyroidism: elevated TSH; correct before labeling primary dyslipidemia
Nephrotic syndrome: heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia; treat renal cause

table.title: Risk-based primary prevention and secondary target

essential-hypertension.name: Essential hypertension
essential-hypertension.scope: Blood pressure staging, nonpharmacologic interventions (weight loss, DASH, exercise), first-line antihypertensive agents, resistant hypertension
essential-hypertension.core: Persistently elevated arterial pressure usually reflects multifactorial primary hypertension; confirm accurate repeated measurements before long-term treatment decisions.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, family history, obesity, excess sodium/alcohol, inactivity, poor sleep
NSAIDs, stimulants, oral contraceptives can raise BP; assess before labeling primary disease

rows.label: Clues
items: Usually asymptomatic; headache alone does not establish hypertensive emergency
★ **Acute target-organ injury** with severe pressure → hypertensive emergency; BP number alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased vascular resistance, altered renal sodium handling, sympathetic/RAAS activation sustain elevated pressure
Chronic endothelial injury accelerates atherosclerosis and small-vessel organ damage

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Average ≥2 readings on ≥2 visits; confirm using **home BP or ambulatory monitoring**
Rest seated, feet supported, correct cuff, arm at heart level; avoid recent caffeine/exercise
BMP, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis/albuminuria, lipids, glucose/A1c, ECG assess risk and injury
Resistant: above goal on 3 agents including diuretic, or controlled on ≥4; exclude pseudoresistance

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **DASH diet, weight reduction, sodium restriction, aerobic activity**, moderate alcohol; target generally <130/80
≥140/90 → drugs, usually two classes; ≥130/80 with CVD, diabetes, CKD, or PREVENT ≥7.5% → drugs
★ Low-risk stage 1: **3–6 months lifestyle**, then drugs if still ≥130/80; updated 2025 threshold
Initial: chlorthalidone, amlodipine, lisinopril, or losartan; albuminuric CKD → ACE inhibitor/ARB
Resistant after optimized triple regimen → spironolactone; monitor K/creatinine; never combine ACE inhibitor + ARB

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, LV hypertrophy/HF, CKD, retinopathy, aortic disease
Thiazide: low Na/K, gout; ACE inhibitor: cough/angioedema; RAAS drugs contraindicated in pregnancy

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication adherence, home readings, regular follow-up; assess orthostatic symptoms in older adults

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: office high, home normal
Masked hypertension: elevated out-of-office only; secondary causes: abrupt/refractory pressure with renal/endocrine clues

foodborne-illnesses.name: Foodborne illnesses
foodborne-illnesses.scope: Staphylococcus aureus enterotoxin, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens, scombroid, ciguatera, Salmonella, Campylobacter
foodborne-illnesses.core: Incubation time and the dominant symptom separate preformed-toxin vomiting from intestinal infection requiring selective stool testing and antibiotics.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Food improperly refrigerated/reheated; shared-meal outbreaks; raw poultry/eggs, unpasteurized dairy, undercooked meat
Infancy, older age, immunosuppression or vascular disease increase invasive Salmonella risk
Improperly chilled tuna/mackerel → scombroid; tropical reef fish → ciguatera

rows.label: Clues
items: Abrupt short-lived emesis without fever favors ingested toxin; inflammatory enteritis → fever or bloody stools
★ **Severe dehydration, bacteremia signs or persistent bloody diarrhea** → urgent assessment
Campylobacter pain may mimic appendicitis; poultry exposure supports both major invasive enteric pathogens
Fish toxins: scombroid → flushing/urticaria; ciguatera → paresthesias, hot/cold temperature reversal

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ingested enterotoxins act rapidly; scombroid: histamine; ciguatoxin activates voltage-gated sodium channels
Invasive mucosal infection induces inflammation and can permit bloodstream spread

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Mild brief outbreak illness → **clinical diagnosis**, usually no stool studies
Fever, bloody/mucoid stool, severe tenderness or sepsis → stool PCR/culture including Shiga toxin testing
Suspected bacteremia → blood cultures; report suspected outbreaks to public health

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Scombroid → **diphenhydramine/famotidine**; anaphylaxis → epinephrine; ciguatera → supportive care
Oral rehydration; severe dehydration → IV isotonic fluids; toxin syndromes do not benefit from antibiotics
Campylobacter severe/prolonged or high-risk illness → azithromycin; most mild cases resolve untreated
Nontyphoidal Salmonella: severe/invasive or high-risk host → ceftriaxone or susceptibility-directed antibiotic
★ Suspected **STEC → avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs**; hemolytic uremic syndrome risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Campylobacter → Guillain-Barré, reactive arthritis; Salmonella → bacteremia, vascular infection, sickle-cell osteomyelitis
Volume depletion → AKI; antibiotics may prolong uncomplicated Salmonella carriage

rows.label: Prevention
items: Cook poultry/eggs thoroughly; separate raw foods, rapid refrigeration, handwashing; avoid unpasteurized products

rows.label: Mimics
items: Norovirus: contagious outbreak with vomiting and diarrhea
Appendicitis: focal progressive peritoneal findings; toxin illness usually self-limited

foodborne-illnesses.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC marine toxins](https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-book/hcp/environmental-hazards-risks/food-poisoning-from-marine-toxins.html), CDC Salmonella/Campylobacter and IDSA infectious-diarrhea guidance.

glomerulonephritis.name: Glomerulonephritis
glomerulonephritis.scope: Nephritic syndrome, poststreptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive GN (anti-GBM, ANCA), lupus nephritis, RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs, proteinuria quantification, kidney biopsy
glomerulonephritis.core: Glomerular inflammation causes hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, edema, and reduced filtration; rapidly rising creatinine demands urgent evaluation for crescentic disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Recent streptococcal pharyngitis/skin infection, systemic autoimmunity, small-vessel vasculitis
IgA nephropathy often follows mucosal infection; anti-GBM pulmonary bleeding risk increases with smoking

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs** identify a glomerular bleeding source
Tea-colored urine, oliguria, periorbital swelling; nephrotic-range protein loss can coexist
★ **Hemoptysis + AKI** → pulmonary–renal syndrome; rapidly progressive disease may initially lack systemic symptoms

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Immune complexes, basement-membrane antibodies, or pauci-immune vascular injury inflame glomerular capillaries
Crescent formation compresses capillary tufts → rapid, potentially irreversible loss of filtration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Urinalysis/microscopy → **creatinine, electrolytes, urine protein/creatinine ratio**; monitor urine output
C3/C4, ANA/dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM; ASO/anti-DNase B when poststreptococcal disease suspected
★ **Kidney biopsy** for rapidly progressive AKI, substantial persistent proteinuria, or uncertain systemic GN
Typical childhood poststreptococcal course may not require biopsy; persistent low C3 beyond 8 weeks warrants reassessment

rows.label: Tx
items: Salt restriction, loop diuretics for overload, BP control; ACE inhibitor/ARB for persistent proteinuria when stable
★ Pulmonary–renal/RPGN → **urgent nephrology, steroids + immunosuppression** before irreversible decline
Anti-GBM: plasma exchange + cyclophosphamide; ANCA: rituximab/cyclophosphamide; plasma exchange only selected severe cases
Lupus: biopsy-directed mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide + steroids; poststreptococcal disease mainly supportive

rows.label: Complications
items: Hyperkalemia, pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency, CKD; dialysis for refractory life-threatening derangements
Immunosuppression → infection, cytopenias, infertility with cyclophosphamide

rows.label: Prevention
items: Control BP/proteinuria, avoid nephrotoxins, follow renal function and urine findings

rows.label: Mimics
items: ATN: muddy-brown casts after ischemia/toxins
Urologic bleeding: isomorphic RBCs, clots, no RBC casts

glomerulonephritis.evidence: Not checked online; established nephrology teaching.

heat-related-illness.name: Heat-related illness
heat-related-illness.scope: Heat exhaustion, classic and exertional heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia and NMS contrast
heat-related-illness.core: Heat exposure with neurologic dysfunction signals heat stroke, requiring immediate cooling before laboratory confirmation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Classic: older adults, heat waves, impaired sweating, anticholinergics, limited water access
Exertional: strenuous activity, poor acclimatization, heavy equipment, stimulant use

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Delirium, seizures, or coma** distinguish heat stroke from uncomplicated heat exhaustion
Tachycardia, hypotension, vomiting; sweating may persist despite severe heat injury
Core temperature often >40 °C; lower readings after cooling do not exclude heat stroke

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Heat production exceeds dissipation → endothelial injury, systemic inflammation, cellular dysfunction
Sweat losses → hypovolemia; excessive free water intake can produce hyponatremia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Rectal temperature**; oral, axillary, and tympanic measurements may underestimate severity
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CK, urinalysis, liver enzymes, coagulation studies; repeat for evolving injury

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, remove clothing, **rapid whole-body cooling**; do not delay for transport or tests
Exertional: cold-water immersion preferred; classic: evaporative cooling practical; stop active cooling near 39 °C
★ **IV isotonic crystalloid** for hypovolemia; benzodiazepines for seizures or shivering
Avoid antipyretics; environmental hyperthermia has no elevated hypothalamic temperature set point

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, DIC, hepatic failure, ARDS, persistent neurologic deficits
Delayed liver injury despite initial clinical improvement

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Gradual acclimatization**, scheduled rest, shade, hydration, cooling access
Avoid strenuous exercise during peak heat; monitor vulnerable adults during heat waves

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sepsis: infectious focus, fever unrelated to environmental load
Serotonin syndrome: serotonergic exposure, clonus, hyperreflexia

heat-related-illness.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency medicine teaching.

herpes-simplex-virus.name: Herpes simplex virus
herpes-simplex-virus.scope: HSV-1 and HSV-2, genital herpes, neonatal herpes, herpes labialis, eczema herpeticum, acyclovir
herpes-simplex-virus.core: Painful grouped vesicles recurring at mucocutaneous sites reflect latent HSV reactivation; neonatal infection and disseminated disease require urgent systemic treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin/mucosal contact, asymptomatic shedding, new sexual partners; either HSV type can cause genital disease
Immunosuppression, atopic dermatitis; neonatal risk highest with newly acquired maternal infection near delivery

rows.label: Clues
items: Primary genital episode: fever, tender nodes, dysuria, multiple painful ulcers; recurrences generally milder
Labialis: tingling prodrome around lip; herpetic whitlow: painful finger vesicles
★ **Monomorphic punched-out erosions in eczema** → eczema herpeticum; ocular symptoms threaten vision
Neonate: sepsislike illness, vesicles sometimes absent; seizures/hepatitis suggest CNS or disseminated disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: HSV establishes sensory ganglion latency; stress, illness, UV exposure trigger reactivation
Genital HSV-2 recurs and sheds more frequently than genital HSV-1

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Active lesion → **HSV PCR/NAAT with typing**; culture less sensitive as lesions heal
CSF HSV PCR for encephalitis/neonatal CNS concern; early negative may require repeat testing
Neonate → lesion/surface, blood, CSF testing plus liver enzymes; start treatment while testing
Type-specific serology only selected situations; no routine population screening or HSV IgM

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First genital episode → **oral acyclovir or valacyclovir for 7–10 days**
Recurrence → prompt episodic dosing at prodrome; frequent/distressing episodes → daily suppressive valacyclovir
★ Neonatal, CNS, disseminated disease or severe eczema herpeticum → **IV acyclovir**; neonatal duration below
Genital HSV pregnancy: suppress acyclovir/valacyclovir from 36 weeks; lesions/prodrome at labor → cesarean
Corneal involvement → urgent ophthalmology; avoid unsupervised ocular corticosteroids

rows.label: Complications
items: Encephalitis, aseptic meningitis, urinary retention, keratitis, dissemination; increased HIV acquisition risk
Acyclovir → crystal nephropathy, neurotoxicity with renal impairment; hydration and dose adjustment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Avoid sex during lesions/prodrome**, condoms, partner disclosure; suppression lowers but never eliminates transmission
Avoid kissing infants with active labialis; cover lesions, hand hygiene

rows.label: Mimics
items: Syphilis: classically painless chancre
Aphthae: mucosal ulcers without preceding grouped vesicles
Zoster: unilateral dermatomal eruption rather than recurrent focal mucocutaneous clusters

herpes-simplex-virus.evidence: Checked genital disease 2026-10-30: [CDC HSV guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/herpes.htm); neonatal/eczema management established teaching.

table.title: Neonatal IV acyclovir duration
rows: ≥21 days; CNS: confirm CSF PCR clearance

hiv-infection.name: HIV infection
hiv-infection.scope: Acute HIV, testing, ART start, opportunistic infection prophylaxis, PrEP/PEP, opportunistic infections (CMV retinitis, toxoplasmosis, PJP)
hiv-infection.core: HIV progressively depletes CD4 cells; early diagnosis and suppressive ART prevent immune failure and sexual transmission.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual exposure, shared injection equipment, perinatal transmission; other STIs increase acquisition risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute infection: fever, rash, sore throat, generalized lymphadenopathy after recent exposure
Weight loss, oral thrush, recurrent infections suggest advanced immunodeficiency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Retroviral integration creates lifelong reservoirs; ongoing replication drives immune depletion and inflammation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Fourth-generation Ag/Ab → HIV-1/2 differentiation assay**; discordance → HIV RNA
★ Recent exposure/acute syndrome despite negative screen → **HIV RNA**, before antibodies appear
Baseline viral load, CD4, resistance genotype, renal/liver function, HBV/HCV/TB testing; pregnancy assessment
AIDS: CD4 <200 or AIDS-defining illness regardless of count

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Start **integrase-based ART promptly**, usually bictegravir/TAF/emtricitabine; assess HBV coinfection and interactions
Do not delay routine ART for genotype; cryptococcal/TB meningitis require disease-specific deferred timing
PJP: TMP-SMX; add glucocorticoid if PaO₂ <70 or A–a gradient ≥35
Toxoplasmosis: pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin or TMP-SMX; CMV retinitis: valganciclovir, urgent ophthalmology

rows.label: Complications
items: Opportunistic infections, malignancies, wasting, neurocognitive disease, kidney disease
Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome after ART; drug toxicity/interactions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ PJP prophylaxis: **TMP-SMX** with CD4 <200 before/starting ART; on ART, <100 or 100–200 with viremia
Toxoplasma IgG positive + CD4 <100 → prophylaxis; MAC <50 only without immediate effective ART
★ Exposure ≤72 hours → **28-day PEP: dolutegravir + TDF/emtricitabine**; do not delay for laboratory results
PrEP: TDF/emtricitabine, cabotegravir, or lenacapavir; exclude HIV first, continue serial testing

rows.label: Mimics
items: EBV mononucleosis: atypical lymphocytes, heterophile positivity; acute HIV can be heterophile-negative
Primary CNS lymphoma: often solitary brain lesion, fails empiric anti-Toxoplasma treatment

table.title: Advanced-disease syndromes
rows: Dry cough, hypoxemia, ground-glass; induced sputum/BAL

hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.name: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis
hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.scope: Bird fancier lung, farmer lung, acute vs chronic presentation, antigen avoidance, centrilobular ground-glass nodules on HRCT, systemic corticosteroids
hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.core: Immune-mediated small-airway and interstitial lung disease follows inhaled antigen exposure; identifying and removing the exposure is central to treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Bird proteins from pets, feathers, droppings; moldy hay in farming
Damp buildings, contaminated humidifiers/hot tubs, occupational organic dust; ask about home and hobbies

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Recurrent **cough, dyspnea, fever hours after exposure**, improvement away from source
Chronic exposure: insidious exertional limitation, weight loss, dry inspiratory crackles; clubbing with fibrosis
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, falling exercise saturation indicate substantial impairment; chronic disease may lack febrile episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Repeated antigen inhalation triggers immune-complex and T-cell responses around bronchioles and alveoli
Persistent inflammation produces poorly formed noncaseating granulomas and potentially irreversible fibrosis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Exposure history + HRCT**: centrilobular ground-glass nodules, mosaic attenuation, expiratory air trapping
Fibrotic disease: reticulation, traction bronchiectasis ± honeycombing; distribution can differ from basal-predominant IPF
PFTs: restriction and ↓DLCO, sometimes mixed obstruction; BAL lymphocytosis supports diagnosis
Serum antigen-specific IgG documents sensitization, **not disease**; absence does not exclude
Multidisciplinary review; biopsy only when exposure, imaging, and BAL leave clinically important uncertainty

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Complete antigen avoidance** and environmental remediation; respirator alone may be insufficient
★ Severe symptomatic nonfibrotic disease → **systemic glucocorticoids** to accelerate recovery
Oxygen for hypoxemia, pulmonary rehabilitation; progressive fibrotic disease → specialist antifibrotic consideration
Advanced refractory fibrosis → lung transplant evaluation; antibiotics do not treat sterile immune inflammation

rows.label: Complications
items: Progressive fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, chronic respiratory failure, cor pulmonale
Symptoms can persist despite avoidance once irreversible structural damage has occurred

rows.label: Prevention
items: Remove birds/mold sources, maintain ventilation, control workplace organic-dust exposure
Counsel household members about ongoing feather products or hidden dampness; monitor lung function after removal

rows.label: Mimics
items: IPF: older adult, basal subpleural honeycombing, no explanatory antigen
Sarcoidosis: well-formed granulomas, hilar adenopathy, extrapulmonary involvement
Organic dust toxic syndrome: heavy exposure, acute flu-like illness without antigen-specific sensitization

hypersensitivity-pneumonitis.evidence: Not checked online; established ATS diagnostic and management teaching.

hyperthyroidism.name: Hyperthyroidism and thyrotoxicosis
hyperthyroidism.scope: Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, toxic adenoma, subacute thyroiditis, thyroid storm, beta-blockers, thionamides, radioactive iodine
hyperthyroidism.core: Excess circulating thyroid hormone → heat intolerance, weight loss despite appetite, tremor, and tachycardia; hormone overproduction differs from destructive release.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Autoimmune history, female sex; older age favors autonomous nodules
Iodine load, amiodarone, exogenous thyroid hormone; infection/surgery can precipitate storm

rows.label: Clues
items: Hyperreflexia, frequent stools, proximal weakness, widened pulse pressure; older adults may have apathetic presentation
★ **Thyroid storm**: fever, delirium, severe tachyarrhythmia, vomiting, heart failure; clinical diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Increased tissue metabolic activity and beta-adrenergic sensitivity explain systemic manifestations
Thionamides block thyroid peroxidase; PTU also reduces peripheral T4 → T3 conversion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **TSH first → free T4**, total T3 if T4 normal; suppressed TSH with elevated hormones
TRAb establishes Graves; uncertain cause → radioactive iodine uptake, except pregnancy/lactation
Low uptake: thyroiditis/exogenous hormone; low thyroglobulin supports exogenous ingestion

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptom control: **propranolol**; caution in asthma or decompensated HF
★ Storm → ICU, cooling/fluids, beta-blockade if tolerated, **PTU → iodine ≥1 hour later**, hydrocortisone
Radioiodine contraindicated during pregnancy/lactation; significant active orbitopathy favors another definitive treatment
Compression/suspicious nodule → thyroidectomy after control; pregnancy: first-trimester PTU, later methimazole

rows.label: Complications
items: AF, embolism, osteoporosis, cardiomyopathy; radioiodine often → hypothyroidism
★ Thionamides: **fever/sore throat → stop drug, urgent CBC**; PTU → severe hepatotoxicity

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor free T4 early during treatment; TSH recovery lags
Smoking cessation for orbitopathy; definitive treatment before planned pregnancy when feasible

rows.label: Mimics
items: Panic disorder: episodic symptoms without thyroid biochemical abnormalities
Pheochromocytoma: paroxysmal headache, sweating, severe hypertension
Menopause: hot flashes with menstrual transition, normal thyroid testing

table.title: Etiology determines treatment
rows: Diffuse uptake; bruit, orbitopathy, pretibial myxedema
One hot nodule, suppressed surrounding tissue
NSAID; prednisone if severe; no thionamides

hypocalcemia.name: Hypocalcemia
hypocalcemia.scope: Hypoparathyroidism, vitamin D deficiency, post-thyroidectomy, hypomagnesemia
hypocalcemia.core: Low ionized calcium causes neuromuscular irritability and QT prolongation; severe symptoms require IV calcium while the cause is corrected.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Thyroid/parathyroid surgery, autoimmune hypoparathyroidism, DiGeorge syndrome
Vitamin D deficiency from low intake, malabsorption, limited sun; CKD, pancreatitis, massive citrate transfusion
Severe hypomagnesemia from alcoholism, diarrhea, PPIs, diuretics; bisphosphonates/denosumab can precipitate deficiency

rows.label: Clues
items: Perioral tingling, distal paresthesias, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm
★ **Trousseau sign**: cuff-induced carpal spasm; Chvostek sign is less specific
★ Severe: **seizures, laryngospasm, arrhythmias**; ECG shows prolonged QT
Post-thyroidectomy tingling or stridor requires immediate calcium assessment rather than simple reassurance

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers nerve excitation threshold; myocardial repolarization is prolonged
Low magnesium impairs both PTH secretion and action, making calcium replacement alone ineffective

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Ionized calcium**, Mg, phosphate, creatinine, PTH, 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Low albumin lowers total calcium, not necessarily ionized; correction formulas unreliable in critical illness
Alkalosis increases albumin binding → symptomatic low ionized calcium despite unchanged total concentration
Interpret PTH relative to calcium: normal PTH can be inappropriately low during hypocalcemia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Symptomatic, severe, or ECG changes → **IV calcium gluconate with ECG monitoring**
Mild stable disease → oral calcium; nutritional vitamin D deficiency → cholecalciferol/ergocalciferol
Hypoparathyroidism or advanced CKD → **calcitriol** plus calcium; coordinate phosphate management
★ **Replace magnesium** when deficient; correct underlying cause, avoid overcorrection

rows.label: Complications
items: Tetany, seizures, ventricular arrhythmias; chronic deficiency can cause cataracts and basal ganglia calcification
Overreplacement → hypercalciuria, nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis; monitor serum and urine calcium

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor calcium after neck surgery and antiresorptive treatment; ensure sufficient vitamin D/calcium intake
Chronic hypoparathyroidism: target symptom control with low-normal serum calcium, avoiding renal calcium loading

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hyperventilation syndrome: transient alkalosis-related ionized reduction; assess precipitating illness
Seizure disorder: no biochemical calcium explanation; pseudohypocalcemia: normal ionized level

hypocalcemia.evidence: Not checked online; established endocrine teaching.

inflammatory-bowel-disease.name: Inflammatory bowel disease
inflammatory-bowel-disease.scope: Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, extraintestinal manifestations (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, uveitis), toxic megacolon, colorectal cancer risk, biologic therapy
inflammatory-bowel-disease.core: Chronic relapsing intestinal inflammation: Crohn disease affects any gastrointestinal segment; ulcerative colitis begins in the rectum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Family history, young adulthood; smoking worsens Crohn disease
NSAIDs and enteric infections can precipitate flares

rows.label: Clues
items: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, weight loss, anemia; children may have growth failure
Arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum; PSC particularly associated with UC
★ Severe colitis: fever, tachycardia, frequent bloody stools; distention suggests **toxic megacolon**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Dysregulated mucosal immune response to intestinal microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stool **C. difficile** testing and cultures before attributing worsening diarrhea to inflammation
Fecal calprotectin supports intestinal inflammation; **ileocolonoscopy with biopsies** confirms
Suspected small-bowel disease or abscess → MR enterography; avoid capsule with suspected stricture
Fulminant colitis → abdominal radiograph and limited sigmoidoscopy; avoid full colonoscopy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute severe UC → hospitalization, **IV methylprednisolone**, fluids, VTE prophylaxis
Steroid-refractory severe UC → infliximab or cyclosporine; perforation or megacolon → urgent colectomy
★ Steroids induce remission only; **never maintenance**
Crohn abscess → antibiotics and drainage before immunosuppression

rows.label: Complications
items: Fistulas, strictures, obstruction and B12 deficiency in Crohn; colectomy does not cure Crohn
Colonic disease → colorectal cancer; active inflammation → venous thromboembolism

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Colonic disease → surveillance colonoscopy beginning about **8 years** after onset; PSC → immediately
Vaccinate and screen TB/HBV before biologics; smoking cessation for Crohn

rows.label: Mimics
items: IBS: no bleeding, weight loss or inflammatory markers
Ischemic colitis: abrupt pain followed by hematochezia, vascular risk

inguinal-hernia.name: Inguinal hernia
inguinal-hernia.scope: Direct inguinal hernia, indirect inguinal hernia, femoral hernia, incarcerated and strangulated hernia, physical exam, elective vs emergent surgical repair
inguinal-hernia.core: A groin bulge enlarging with strain suggests hernia; a painful irreducible mass with obstructive or ischemic signs requires urgent surgical assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Male sex, family history, prematurity, persistent processus vaginalis
Age-related fascial weakness, chronic cough, constipation, heavy strain; femoral hernias more frequent in women

rows.label: Clues
items: Bulge or dragging discomfort with standing/Valsalva, improving supine or after reduction
Incarcerated: contents cannot be reduced; bowel obstruction causes vomiting, distention, obstipation
★ **Severe persistent pain**, tenderness, erythema, toxicity/peritonitis → impaired perfusion; fever may be late

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Abdominal contents protrude through a weak opening; a narrow neck impairs venous then arterial perfusion
Richter hernia traps only bowel-wall segment; ischemia may occur without complete obstruction

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Standing groin examination with cough/Valsalva**; inspect both sides and assess reducibility
Uncertain occult lesion → dynamic ultrasound; CT if obstruction, complication, or alternative diagnosis suspected
Clinical strangulation → immediate operation; imaging must not delay treatment
Do not rely on surface examination alone to reliably distinguish direct from indirect anatomy

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Strangulation → **IV fluids, NPO, analgesia, antibiotics, emergency repair**; resect nonviable bowel
Incarceration without ischemic features → urgent surgeon evaluation; gentle reduction only in selected cases
★ Symptomatic inguinal hernia → **elective mesh repair** in adults; children → herniotomy
Minimally symptomatic men may choose watchful waiting with return precautions
Women and femoral hernias → timely repair because occult femoral disease and strangulation risk are greater

rows.label: Complications
items: Bowel obstruction, ischemic necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Repair → chronic groin pain, recurrence, wound/mesh infection, testicular ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat constipation and chronic cough, smoking cessation, weight management; risk reduction cannot close an existing defect
After reduction or observation: urgent return for escalating pain, vomiting, or loss of reducibility

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lymphadenopathy: discrete solid nodes without cough impulse
Hydrocele: transilluminates; confined fluid rather than reducible bowel
Saphena varix: compressible venous swelling; Doppler demonstrates venous flow

table.title: Anatomic distinctions
rows: Below inguinal ligament, medial femoral vein

lung-cancer.name: Lung cancer
lung-cancer.scope: Non-small cell, small cell, paraneoplastic syndromes, Pancoast, screening
lung-cancer.core: Persistent cough, hemoptysis, weight loss, or a suspicious lung lesion requires tissue diagnosis and staging before treatment selection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, radon, asbestos, occupational carcinogens, prior thoracic radiation; adenocarcinoma also occurs in never-smokers

rows.label: Clues
items: Recurrent focal pneumonia, hoarseness, clubbing, unexplained pleural effusion
★ **Pancoast tumor**: shoulder/ulnar-arm pain + ipsilateral Horner syndrome
SVC obstruction: facial swelling, neck-vein distention; cord compression or airway compromise requires urgent action

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bronchogenic malignant transformation → local invasion, lymphatic spread, hematogenous metastasis
Ectopic hormone production and immune cross-reactivity cause paraneoplastic syndromes

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Suspicious finding → **contrast chest CT**; biopsy easiest site that establishes highest stage
Central lesion/nodes → bronchoscopy/EBUS; peripheral lesion → CT-guided biopsy; effusion → cytology
PET/CT for extracranial staging, brain MRI for selected stages/small-cell disease; pulmonary function before resection
Molecular profiling and PD-L1 guide advanced NSCLC treatment; suspicious nodes often require pathologic staging

rows.label: Tx
