items: ★ Early operable NSCLC → **surgical resection + nodal evaluation**; inoperable localized → stereotactic radiation
Locally advanced NSCLC → combined systemic treatment/radiation ± surgery in selected patients
Metastatic NSCLC → biomarker-directed agents or immunotherapy/chemotherapy
★ Small-cell → **platinum + etoposide**, stage-dependent radiation/immunotherapy; surgery rarely used

rows.label: Complications
items: Brain/bone/adrenal/liver metastases, malignant effusion, thrombosis, respiratory failure
Radiation pneumonitis; checkpoint inhibitors → immune pneumonitis/endocrinopathies

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ USPSTF: **annual low-dose CT**, age 50–80, ≥20 pack-years, current smoking or quit <15 years
Stop after 15 quit-years or limited curative candidacy; **ACS omits quit-time restriction**
Smoking cessation and radon mitigation; chest radiographs do not substitute for screening CT

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB/fungal granuloma: microbiologic evidence; PET uptake not specific for cancer
Hamartoma: fat/popcorn calcification; pneumonia: clinical/radiographic response to antibiotics

lung-cancer.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2021](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening), [ACS 2023 guideline](https://acsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.3322/caac.21811); treatment: established stage-based framework.

microcytic-anemia.name: Microcytic anemia
microcytic-anemia.scope: Iron deficiency, anemia of chronic disease, thalassemia, sideroblastic anemia
microcytic-anemia.core: Low hemoglobin with MCV <80 fL: distinguish depleted iron, inflammatory iron sequestration, globin underproduction, and defective heme synthesis.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Menstrual/GI blood loss, pregnancy, low intake, malabsorption → iron depletion
Chronic infection, autoimmune disease, malignancy → inflammatory anemia
Inherited hemoglobin disorders; alcohol, lead, isoniazid, myelodysplasia → disordered heme production

rows.label: Clues
items: Fatigue, pallor, exertional dyspnea; severe anemia → tachycardia, angina, syncope
Pica, koilonychia, restless legs suggest iron deficiency
Markedly low MCV with relatively preserved hemoglobin and high RBC count suggests thalassemia trait

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflammation → ↑hepcidin → ferroportin suppression, impaired absorption and iron release
Sideroblasts: mitochondrial iron accumulation in erythroblasts from impaired protoporphyrin synthesis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear → ferritin**, iron, TIBC, transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation
★ Ferritin **<45 ng/mL in anemia** supports iron deficiency; normal result cannot exclude during inflammation
★ Adult men/postmenopausal women with iron deficiency → **EGD + colonoscopy**; consider celiac testing
Hemoglobin electrophoresis for suspected beta-thalassemia; alpha trait may require genetic testing; exposure → blood lead

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Iron deficiency → **oral ferrous sulfate**; intolerance/malabsorption or rapid replacement need → IV iron
Treat bleeding source; continue iron about 3 months beyond hemoglobin normalization; reassess nonresponse
Inflammatory anemia → treat underlying disease; selected CKD → iron ± erythropoietin
Sideroblastic: remove trigger, pyridoxine if isoniazid-related; severe thalassemia → transfusion/chelation

rows.label: Complications
items: Iron deficiency: developmental effects in children, adverse pregnancy outcomes
Repeated transfusion → iron overload, cardiac/hepatic injury; oral iron → constipation, dark stool

rows.label: Prevention
items: Adequate dietary iron, pregnancy supplementation, lead-exposure reduction
★ **No empiric long-term iron for thalassemia trait** without documented deficiency

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute blood loss: initially normocytic; hemoglobin may lag volume loss
Hemolysis: reticulocytosis, ↑LDH/indirect bilirubin, ↓haptoglobin

microcytic-anemia.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [AGA iron deficiency evaluation 2020](https://gastro.org/clinical-guidance/gastrointestinal-evaluation-of-iron-deficiency-anemia/); remaining hematology established teaching.

myeloproliferative-neoplasms.name: Myeloproliferative neoplasms
myeloproliferative-neoplasms.scope: CML, polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, primary myelofibrosis
myeloproliferative-neoplasms.core: Clonal marrow proliferation elevates mature blood-cell counts or causes progressive fibrosis; thrombosis and transformation drive management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Usually acquired stem-cell mutations in adults; age and prior thrombosis predict vascular risk
Prior radiation exposure associated with CML; no common lifestyle trigger explains most cases

rows.label: Clues
items: Splenomegaly, fatigue, early satiety, constitutional symptoms; markedly abnormal CBC may be incidental
★ **Aquagenic pruritus**, erythromelalgia or unexplained splanchnic thrombosis → evaluate clonal disease
Very high platelets may paradoxically cause mucosal bleeding through acquired von Willebrand dysfunction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Constitutive tyrosine-kinase signaling produces growth independent of normal feedback
Myelofibrosis → cytokine-driven fibrosis and extramedullary hematopoiesis; not simply excess fibroblast clonality

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CBC/smear**, erythropoietin with erythrocytosis; marrow biopsy and mutation testing classify disease
PV thresholds: hemoglobin >16.5 g/dL men/>16 women or hematocrit >49%/>48%, with diagnostic context
ET requires persistent platelets ≥450,000/µL plus marrow/molecular findings and exclusion of reactive causes
Teardrops and leukoerythroblastosis support fibrosis; marrow aspiration may yield dry tap

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ PV → **phlebotomy to hematocrit <45%** plus low-dose aspirin if safe
PV/ET high thrombotic risk → hydroxyurea; interferon favored for selected younger/pregnant patients
★ CML → **BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase inhibitor**, e.g., imatinib; monitor molecular response
Symptomatic myelofibrosis → JAK inhibitor such as ruxolitinib; allogeneic transplant potentially curative
Extreme thrombocytosis with bleeding → assess von Willebrand function before aspirin; urgent cytoreduction if critical

rows.label: Complications
items: Arterial/venous thrombosis, hemorrhage, hyperuricemia; secondary myelofibrosis or AML
CML blast phase: ≥20% blasts; advanced disease needs acute-leukemia-directed specialist treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Cardiovascular risk control; disease-specific count control, pregnancy planning, monitor progression

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reactive thrombocytosis: iron deficiency/inflammation; secondary erythrocytosis: hypoxia or ↑EPO
Leukemoid reaction: toxic granulation, infection trigger, absent BCR-ABL

myeloproliferative-neoplasms.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical teaching.

osteoarthritis.name: Osteoarthritis
osteoarthritis.scope: Clinical diagnosis (Heberden/Bouchard nodes, activity-related pain), radiographic findings, nonpharmacologic therapy, oral and topical NSAIDs, injections
osteoarthritis.core: Activity-related joint pain with brief morning stiffness, crepitus and bony enlargement suggests degenerative joint disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, obesity, prior trauma, malalignment, repetitive occupational loading
Family history, particularly hand disease; obesity affects both mechanical and metabolic risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Morning stiffness generally **<30 minutes**; pain improves with rest early in disease
Knees, hips, first carpometacarpal, DIP and PIP commonly involved; MCP usually spared
Heberden nodes: DIP; Bouchard nodes: PIP; reduced motion and varus/valgus deformity
Hip disease: groin pain with restricted internal rotation; referred pain can localize to knee

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Articular cartilage loss, subchondral remodeling and osteophytes; low-grade synovial inflammation
Joint pain arises from innervated surrounding structures rather than aneural cartilage itself

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical presentation → **clinical diagnosis**; imaging unnecessary for straightforward mild disease
Weight-bearing radiographs if uncertain/severe: asymmetric joint-space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis/cysts
★ Hot acutely swollen joint → **arthrocentesis**; do not assume OA flare
OA fluid noninflammatory: usually WBC <2000/µL; inflammatory markers generally normal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ First-line **exercise, strengthening, weight loss**; cane contralateral to painful hip/knee
★ Knee/hand pain → **topical diclofenac**; oral NSAID if insufficient and renal/GI/CV risks acceptable
Acetaminophen for selected patients unable to use NSAIDs; duloxetine for persistent pain
Intra-articular glucocorticoid for short-term relief; avoid routine opioids and hyaluronic acid injections
Severe pain/function loss despite conservative treatment → **joint replacement**

rows.label: Complications
items: Functional limitation, falls, reduced activity and secondary deconditioning
NSAIDs → GI bleeding, AKI, fluid retention; arthroplasty → infection or VTE

rows.label: Prevention
items: Healthy weight, muscle conditioning, injury prevention; physical activity does not require complete joint rest

rows.label: Mimics
items: Rheumatoid arthritis: prolonged stiffness, boggy symmetric MCP/wrist synovitis
CPPD: acute inflammatory flares, chondrocalcinosis
Septic arthritis: fever, severe painful passive motion, positive synovial culture

osteoarthritis.evidence: Not checked online; established ACR/Arthritis Foundation principles.

osteomyelitis.name: Osteomyelitis
osteomyelitis.scope: Vertebral osteomyelitis and discitis, hematogenous seeding (S. aureus, IV drug use), contiguous spread (diabetic foot ulcer), probe-to-bone test, MRI, bone biopsy and culture, parenteral antibiotics
osteomyelitis.core: Persistent focal bone or back pain, especially with bacteremia, a deep diabetic ulcer, or elevated inflammatory markers, suggests bone infection.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Hematogenous seeding: S. aureus, endocarditis, injection drug use; vertebral disease often lacks fever
Contiguous spread: diabetic foot ulcers, pressure injury; direct inoculation: open fracture, surgery, hardware
Sickle cell: Salmonella association, but S. aureus remains important; plantar puncture through shoe → Pseudomonas

rows.label: Clues
items: Point tenderness, swelling, drainage or nonhealing sinus; systemic toxicity may be absent
★ New neurologic deficit, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention → **epidural extension/cord compression**
Diabetic ulcer over bony prominence, visible bone, or prolonged failure to heal increases suspicion

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Infected bone develops inflammatory pressure, vascular compromise, and necrosis
Sequestrum: devitalized infected bone; involucrum: reactive new bone; biofilm promotes hardware persistence

rows.label: Dx
items: CBC, ESR/CRP, two blood-culture sets; plain films first but early findings can be absent
★ Diabetic foot: **probe-to-bone** plus radiographs/inflammatory markers; MRI if diagnosis remains uncertain
★ **MRI** best for early marrow disease and epidural/paraspinal abscess
Bone biopsy for histology/culture before antibiotics if stable; superficial wound swabs unreliable
Compatible vertebral MRI plus S. aureus bacteremia usually obviates biopsy; assess endocarditis source

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Sepsis or neurologic compromise → cultures then **IV vancomycin + cefepime**, urgent surgical assessment
Stable vertebral disease → obtain microbiologic diagnosis before empiric antibiotics
MSSA → cefazolin/nafcillin; MRSA → vancomycin; tailor to cultures, usually about **6 weeks**
IV initially for serious disease; selected stable patients can complete highly bioavailable oral regimens
Debride necrotic bone/drain abscess; surgery for instability, progressive deficit, or uncontrolled infection

rows.label: Complications
items: Epidural abscess, pathologic fracture, deformity, bacteremia, chronic draining sinus
Longstanding sinus may develop squamous carcinoma; prolonged antibiotics → line infection, renal injury, C. difficile

rows.label: Prevention
items: Diabetic foot inspection, offloading, vascular assessment, glucose control; prompt open-fracture antibiotics and debridement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Charcot arthropathy: neuropathic warm foot, joint fragmentation; MRI/biopsy may distinguish overlapping infection
Bone malignancy: destructive mass, pathology without infection
Degenerative disc disease: mechanical pain without infectious endplate/disc pattern

osteoporosis.name: Osteoporosis
osteoporosis.scope: DEXA scan T-score criteria, screening guidelines, glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, vertebral compression fractures, bisphosphonates
osteoporosis.core: Fragility fracture or markedly reduced bone density identifies skeletal weakness, often silent until hip or vertebral fracture.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Postmenopause, older age, low BMI, parental hip fracture, smoking, excess alcohol
Glucocorticoids, hypogonadism, malabsorption, hyperthyroidism, immobility, rheumatoid arthritis

rows.label: Clues
items: Height loss, kyphosis, acute focal back pain after trivial strain suggest vertebral compression
Neurologic deficits, fever, or nocturnal pain suggest alternative spinal pathology

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Bone resorption exceeds formation; microarchitecture deteriorates despite normally mineralized remaining bone
Estrogen deficiency increases osteoclast activity; steroids suppress osteoblasts and reduce calcium balance

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Hip/spine DXA**; use T-scores in postmenopausal women and men ≥50
★ Hip/vertebral low-trauma fracture establishes diagnosis regardless of DXA; image symptomatic vertebral levels
CBC, calcium, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, 25-OH vitamin D; targeted secondary-cause testing
Younger adults: Z-score ≤−2 suggests below-age bone density; T-score alone insufficient

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Alendronate or zoledronic acid** for qualifying fracture, osteoporosis-range DXA, or high FRAX risk
Osteopenia: treat if 10-year hip risk ≥3% or major osteoporotic risk ≥20%
Oral bisphosphonate: fasting water, remain upright; avoid esophageal disease, hypocalcemia, severe kidney dysfunction
Very high risk → teriparatide/romosozumab then antiresorptive; stopping denosumab requires follow-on antiresorptive
Vertebral pain: analgesia, mobilization, short bracing; procedures reserved for selected refractory cases

rows.label: Complications
items: ★ **Hip fracture** → immobility, thromboembolism, excess mortality
Bisphosphonates: rare jaw osteonecrosis/atypical femur fracture; denosumab: hypocalcemia, rebound vertebral fractures

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Screen **women ≥65**, younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; evidence insufficient for routine male screening
Weight-bearing/resistance exercise, fall prevention, adequate dietary calcium/vitamin D; minimize tobacco and alcohol
Prednisone-equivalent ≥2.5 mg/day for >3 months → early fracture-risk assessment and preventive treatment by risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Osteomalacia: defective mineralization, low phosphate, elevated alkaline phosphatase
Myeloma: anemia, renal injury, lytic lesions; metastatic fracture: destructive focal lesion

osteoporosis.evidence: Screening checked 2026-10-30: [USPSTF 2025](https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/osteoporosis-screening%20); treatment: established fracture-risk framework.

otitis-externa.name: Otitis externa
otitis-externa.scope: Acute diffuse otitis externa, swimmer ear prevention, topical fluoroquinolones, necrotizing otitis externa
otitis-externa.core: Otalgia worsened by moving the pinna or pressing the tragus, with an inflamed external canal, indicates otitis externa.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Swimming, moisture, canal trauma from cotton swabs/hearing aids, eczema
Diabetes, older age, immunosuppression → necrotizing infection risk; Pseudomonas often responsible

rows.label: Clues
items: Canal erythema, edema, debris, otorrhea; conductive hearing loss from occlusion
★ **Severe nocturnal pain disproportionate to examination**, granulation tissue → necrotizing otitis externa
Facial weakness or other cranial neuropathy suggests skull-base extension; fever may be absent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Loss of acidic cerumen barrier permits bacterial proliferation; typical organisms Pseudomonas and S aureus
Necrotizing form invades soft tissue and skull base rather than remaining superficial

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Otoscopy + tragal/pinna tenderness**; inspect tympanic membrane when visible
Routine uncomplicated cases require no culture or imaging; refractory infection → culture, assess fungal/dermatologic causes
★ Suspected invasive disease → **ESR/CRP, culture, CT temporal bone ± MRI**
Biopsy suspicious persistent granulation to exclude malignancy; MRI better defines soft tissue/cranial involvement

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Uncomplicated → **topical ofloxacin or ciprofloxacin ± steroid**, usually 7–10 days
Gentle canal cleaning; marked edema → wick to deliver drops; acetaminophen/NSAID for pain
Known/suspected perforation or tubes → nonototoxic fluoroquinolone; avoid aminoglycoside/alcohol drops
No routine oral antibiotic unless extension beyond canal, high-risk host, or inability to deliver topical treatment
★ Necrotizing infection → **urgent ENT + systemic antipseudomonal antibiotics**, often prolonged, culture-directed

rows.label: Complications
items: Periauricular cellulitis, canal stenosis, skull-base osteomyelitis, cranial neuropathy
Persistent pain despite drops → reassess technique, obstruction, wrong organism, invasive disease

rows.label: Prevention
items: Keep ear dry during treatment; avoid canal instrumentation and cotton swabs
After swimming → dry externally; acidifying drops only with intact membrane and no tubes

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute otitis media: middle-ear effusion/bulging TM, little tragal tenderness
Otomycosis: prominent itching, fungal debris, antibiotic-drop history
Mastoiditis: postauricular swelling/tenderness and protruding pinna

otitis-externa.evidence: Not checked online; established otolaryngology topical treatment and invasive-infection principles.

pancreatic-cancer.name: Pancreatic cancer
pancreatic-cancer.scope: Pancreatic adenocarcinoma, painless jaundice, Courvoisier sign, CA 19-9, neuroendocrine tumors (gastrinoma, insulinoma)
pancreatic-cancer.core: Older adult with weight loss and painless obstructive jaundice, or persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, chronic pancreatitis, obesity, increasing age; strong family history, hereditary cancer syndromes
New diabetes with unexplained weight loss can signal occult malignancy

rows.label: Clues
items: Head lesions: dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, nontender palpable gallbladder (**Courvoisier sign**)
Body/tail lesions: late presentation with pain and cachexia; migratory thrombophlebitis may occur

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Ductal adenocarcinoma causes biliary obstruction, perineural invasion, and early metastatic spread
Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from endocrine cells; may be functional or incidental

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pancreatic-protocol CT** for mass, vessels, metastases; ultrasound may initially show biliary dilation
EUS biopsy before systemic treatment/uncertain diagnosis; not mandatory before straightforward resection
★ **CA 19-9** monitors disease; neither screening nor definitive diagnosis; obstruction can falsely elevate
Resectability depends on metastases and major vascular involvement; MRI clarifies indeterminate liver lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Resectable head tumor → **Whipple**; body/tail tumor → distal pancreatectomy; add systemic chemotherapy
Borderline resectable → neoadjuvant treatment; metastatic → systemic treatment and palliation
★ Cholangitis → **urgent ERCP**; unresectable symptomatic jaundice → biliary stent
Analgesia, pancreatic enzymes for malabsorption, nutritional support

rows.label: Complications
items: VTE, biliary infection, gastric outlet obstruction, exocrine insufficiency, diabetes
Resection → pancreatic fistula, delayed gastric emptying, malabsorption

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation; no average-risk population screening; selected hereditary high-risk patients → MRI/EUS surveillance

rows.label: Mimics
items: Choledocholithiasis: colicky pain, ductal stone
Autoimmune pancreatitis: IgG4 elevation, diffuse pancreatic enlargement
Chronic pancreatitis: calcification, recurrent pain, prior inflammation

table.title: Functional neuroendocrine tumors
rows: ↑Insulin/C-peptide during supervised fast; negative sulfonylurea screen

pericardial-disease.name: Pericardial disease
pericardial-disease.scope: Acute pericarditis, pericardial effusion, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis
pericardial-disease.core: Pericardial inflammation, fluid accumulation, or fibrosis produces distinct chest-pain and impaired-filling syndromes; hemodynamic effect depends on accumulation rate.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Viral/idiopathic, autoimmune disease, uremia, malignancy, TB, radiation, cardiac surgery
Early post-MI inflammation or delayed immune-mediated Dressler syndrome; trauma/anticoagulation can cause hemopericardium

rows.label: Clues
items: Pericarditis: sharp pleuritic positional pain, better leaning forward; friction rub may be transient
★ Tamponade: **hypotension, elevated JVP, muffled sounds**, pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg; triad often incomplete
Constrictive disease: edema/ascites, Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, prominent y descent

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Inflamed surfaces cause pain; fluid or scar limits diastolic filling and stroke volume
Tamponade equalizes diastolic pressures; constriction exaggerates ventricular interdependence with respiration

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Pericarditis: ≥2 of **typical pain, rub, diffuse ST elevation/PR depression, new effusion**
Troponin elevation suggests myocardial involvement; CRP supports inflammation; echo assesses fluid and ventricular function
★ **Urgent bedside echo** for suspected tamponade: right-sided chamber collapse, plethoric IVC
Constrictive suspicion → echo, CT/MRI for thickening/calcification; catheterization if diagnosis remains uncertain

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tamponade → **urgent pericardiocentesis**; IV fluids bridge; avoid diuresis/positive-pressure ventilation
Purulent/traumatic effusion or recurrent difficult drainage → surgical drainage/window; antibiotics for bacterial cause
Stable effusion → treat cause, serial echo; low voltage alone never determines drainage
High-risk features → admit: fever, large effusion, immunosuppression, anticoagulation, subacute onset, NSAID failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Recurrent inflammation, arrhythmia/myocarditis, obstructive shock; procedural drainage → cardiac injury
Rapid decompression can rarely cause ventricular dysfunction; NSAIDs → GI/renal injury, colchicine → diarrhea

rows.label: Prevention
items: Colchicine course: first episode 3 months; recurrence ≥6 months; taper anti-inflammatory drugs after remission
Exercise restriction until clinical/inflammatory resolution; optimize dialysis for uremic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: STEMI: regional ST elevation with reciprocal changes; urgent coronary evaluation if uncertain
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: myocardial disease, less respiratory ventricular discordance
PE: thrombotic risk, acute RV strain

table.title: Nonemergency definitive management
rows: Ibuprofen + colchicine; aspirin preferred after MI
Selected low-dose glucocorticoid or IL-1 blockade

polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.name: Polyuria and diabetes insipidus
polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.scope: Central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (lithium, hypercalcemia), water deprivation test, desmopressin response
polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.core: Large-volume dilute urine requires separation of water diuresis from solute diuresis; impaired thirst or water access makes diabetes insipidus dangerous.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Central: sellar surgery/trauma/infiltration; nephrogenic: lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia or inherited defects
Primary polydipsia: excessive voluntary intake, psychiatric disease; osmotic diuresis: diabetes mellitus, mannitol

rows.label: Clues
items: Polyuria >3 L/day in adults, nocturia, polydipsia; distinguish from frequent small-volume voiding
★ **Hypernatremia with urine osmolality <300 mOsm/kg** suggests inadequate antidiuretic effect
Low/low-normal sodium favors excess drinking; dehydration, weakness or altered mentation signals severe water deficit

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Insufficient vasopressin signaling prevents collecting-duct aquaporin-mediated water reabsorption
Lithium enters collecting-duct cells through ENaC and impairs concentrating ability

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **24-hour urine volume**; serum Na/osmolality, urine osmolality, glucose, calcium, K, creatinine
Hyperglycemia with concentrated solute-rich urine → osmotic diuresis; no need for water deprivation
★ Stable hypotonic polyuria → **supervised water deprivation followed by desmopressin**, or stimulated copeptin testing
Avoid dehydration testing in existing hypernatremia/volume depletion; partial defects may yield overlapping responses
Established central disease → pituitary MRI and anterior-axis evaluation; check lithium level with exposure

rows.label: Tx
items: Shock → isotonic resuscitation first; then oral/IV free water with serial sodium monitoring
★ Central → **desmopressin**; avoid excess water intake and monitor for hyponatremia
Nephrogenic → remove cause, low-solute diet, thiazide; lithium-associated → amiloride
Lithium toxicity → stop drug, isotonic fluids; severe neurologic effects/impaired clearance → hemodialysis consultation
Primary polydipsia → address cause and supervised intake plan; desmopressin risks water intoxication

rows.label: Complications
items: Hypernatremic encephalopathy, seizures, hypovolemic shock; overly rapid chronic sodium correction → cerebral edema
Desmopressin/excess drinking → hyponatremic seizures; chronic lithium → CKD

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Reliable water access, sick-day plan; lithium renal/electrolyte monitoring and avoidance of volume depletion

rows.label: Mimics
items: Overactive bladder/UTI: frequency without increased total volume
Postobstructive diuresis: follows relief of retention; monitor fluid/electrolyte losses

polyuria-diabetes-insipidus.evidence: Testing update checked 2026-10-30: [Endotext AVP deficiency/resistance, 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279011/); classic testing patterns: established teaching.

primary-immunodeficiencies.name: Primary immunodeficiencies
primary-immunodeficiencies.scope: Selective IgA deficiency, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), X-linked agammaglobulinemia, severe combined immunodeficiency, hyper-IgE syndrome, Wiskott-Aldrich, chronic granulomatous disease
primary-immunodeficiencies.core: Recurrent, unusually severe, persistent, or opportunistic infections; organism pattern and age of onset localize the immune defect.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Consanguinity, affected relatives, male relatives dying in infancy; absent family history does not exclude disease

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Failure to thrive, chronic diarrhea, persistent thrush, or infections across multiple organ systems
Deep abscesses suggest phagocyte dysfunction; recurrent encapsulated bacteria suggest impaired antibody function

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Selective IgA deficiency: impaired mucosal defense; respiratory infections, giardiasis, atopy, or no symptoms
Antibody disorders impair opsonization; T-cell defects permit viral, fungal, and protozoal opportunists

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Start **CBC with differential, quantitative immunoglobulins**, HIV testing; assess vaccine antibody responses
Lymphocyte subsets distinguish B-cell and T-cell deficiencies; abnormal results → genetic confirmation
IgA deficiency: isolated IgA <7 mg/dL after age 4 years; normal IgG and IgM
★ Newborn **TREC screen** detects impaired T-cell production before symptomatic SCID

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Profound combined immune failure → isolation, irradiated CMV-negative blood products, urgent **transplant evaluation**
Acute infections: organism-directed antimicrobials; immunoglobulin replacement not useful for isolated IgA deficiency

rows.label: Complications
items: Bronchiectasis, chronic enteropathy, autoimmune disease; CVID additionally increases lymphoma risk
Anti-IgA antibodies can cause anaphylaxis to blood products

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Avoid **live vaccines** in major T-cell defects; immunize household contacts with safe vaccine choices
IgA-related transfusion reactions → washed cellular products or IgA-deficient plasma
CGD: TMP-SMX + itraconazole prophylaxis; genetic counseling for inherited defects

rows.label: Mimics
items: HIV: acquired CD4 depletion with positive virologic testing
Secondary hypogammaglobulinemia: nephrotic protein loss, B-cell malignancy, or rituximab exposure

table.title: Defect fingerprints
rows: Adolescent/adult; low IgG, poor vaccine response
Boy after 6 months; absent tonsils/B cells
Infant; absent thymic shadow, profound lymphopenia
Cold abscesses, eczema, retained teeth, pneumatoceles

primary-immunodeficiencies.evidence: Not checked online; established clinical immunology teaching.

pulmonary-hypertension.name: Pulmonary hypertension
pulmonary-hypertension.scope: WHO groups 1-5 (PAH, left heart disease, lung disease/hypoxia, CTEPH, multifactorial), cor pulmonale, echocardiography, right heart catheterization, endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors
pulmonary-hypertension.core: Progressive exertional dyspnea, syncope or right-heart failure with elevated pulmonary pressures requires hemodynamic classification before vasodilator treatment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Connective-tissue disease, congenital shunts, portal hypertension, HIV, methamphetamine → PAH
Left-heart disease, chronic lung disease/hypoxia or prior pulmonary embolism are common secondary contexts

rows.label: Clues
items: Loud P2, RV heave, tricuspid regurgitation murmur; exertional chest pain or presyncope
JVD, hepatomegaly and edema → right-heart failure/cor pulmonale
Severe dyspnea with relatively preserved spirometry or low DLCO suggests pulmonary vascular disease

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pulmonary vascular resistance or elevated left filling pressure increases RV afterload
Sustained pressure overload → RV hypertrophy, dilation, reduced output and systemic venous congestion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Echocardiography** estimates probability and evaluates RV/left-heart function; not definitive pressure diagnosis
★ **Right-heart catheterization: mean PAP >20 mm Hg** at rest confirms PH
Precapillary: wedge ≤15 mm Hg and **PVR >2 Wood units**; postcapillary: wedge >15
★ **V/Q scan** screens CTEPH; normal perfusion essentially excludes chronic thromboembolic disease
PFT/DLCO, chest CT, sleep evaluation, HIV/autoimmune testing by history; vasoreactivity testing in selected PAH

rows.label: Tx
items: Oxygen for hypoxemia, diuresis for congestion; treat underlying disease and refer confirmed PAH/CTEPH
★ PAH → specialist **endothelin antagonist + PDE-5 inhibitor**; high-risk disease → parenteral prostacyclin
Vasoreactive idiopathic/heritable/drug-associated PAH → selected high-dose calcium-channel blocker; not empiric treatment
CTEPH → lifelong anticoagulation and pulmonary endarterectomy if operable; selected balloon angioplasty or riociguat
Do not routinely use PAH vasodilators for left-heart/lung-disease PH; PDE-5 drugs cannot combine with nitrates/riociguat

rows.label: Complications
items: RV failure, arrhythmia, syncope and death; pregnancy carries substantial maternal risk in PAH
Endothelin antagonists are teratogenic; some require liver monitoring

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid methamphetamine, address thromboembolic risk; vaccination, supervised exercise, pregnancy/contraception counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: HFpEF: elevated wedge pressure identifies postcapillary cause
Deconditioning/anemia: no catheter-confirmed pulmonary pressure elevation

rhabdomyolysis.name: Rhabdomyolysis
rhabdomyolysis.scope: Trauma, crush injury, prolonged immobilization, statins, seizures, elevated CK, myoglobinuria (blood on dipstick without RBCs), acute tubular necrosis, aggressive IV saline hydration
rhabdomyolysis.core: Acute skeletal muscle breakdown releases myoglobin and electrolytes; recognize pigment nephropathy early and restore renal perfusion before kidney failure develops.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: ★ **Crush injury, prolonged immobilization**, compartment syndrome, ischemia/reperfusion
Seizures, strenuous exercise, heatstroke, cocaine; statins, especially with interacting drugs
Hypokalemia, infections, alcohol intoxication; pressure injury during unconsciousness

rows.label: Clues
items: Muscle pain, weakness, swelling; dark urine possible, but classic triad often incomplete
↑K, ↑phosphate, early ↓Ca; AST may rise from muscle rather than liver
Tense painful compartment, pain with passive stretch, sensory change → concurrent limb emergency

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Myocyte necrosis → pigment-mediated tubular injury and casts, amplified by hypovolemia and aciduria

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CK >5 times upper limit**, often >1,000 U/L; trend until clearly declining
★ Urine dipstick **heme positive with few/no RBCs** → myoglobin; negative result cannot exclude
Electrolytes, creatinine, ECG, urine output; CK magnitude supports risk assessment, not dialysis alone

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Early **IV normal saline**; titrate to urine output 1–3 mL/kg/hour, avoiding overload
Stop culprit; treat heatstroke/seizures; compartment syndrome → emergency fasciotomy
Hyperkalemic ECG changes → IV calcium, insulin/dextrose; dialysis for refractory electrolyte/volume/acid-base disturbances
★ **No routine bicarbonate or mannitol** for AKI prevention; anuria → reassess fluids, renal consultation
Asymptomatic hypocalcemia → avoid replacement; symptomatic tetany or arrhythmia → calcium

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute tubular necrosis, dangerous arrhythmias, disseminated intravascular coagulation
Recovery phase → rebound hypercalcemia; excessive fluids with renal failure → pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Hydration and gradual exercise progression; avoid exertion during severe heat or illness
Review statin interactions, especially macrolides/gemfibrozil; pressure relief during prolonged immobilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hematuria: numerous RBCs on microscopy
Hemolysis: heme-positive urine with anemia, ↑LDH, ↓haptoglobin rather than marked CK elevation
Inflammatory myopathy: subacute proximal weakness without acute toxic/traumatic trigger

rhabdomyolysis.evidence: Fluid targets and bicarbonate guidance checked 2026-10-30: [AAST consensus, 2022](https://tsaco.bmj.com/content/7/1/e000836.full.pdf).

sarcoidosis.name: Sarcoidosis
sarcoidosis.scope: Noncaseating granulomas, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, pulmonary infiltrates, hypercalcemia, extrapulmonary manifestations (uveitis, erythema nodosum, neurosarcoidosis, cardiac), systemic corticosteroids
sarcoidosis.core: Multisystem granulomatous disease, classically a young adult with bilateral hilar adenopathy; treat threatened organ function rather than an abnormal radiograph alone.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young or middle-aged adults; higher prevalence and disease burden among Black Americans
Familial predisposition; environmental antigen exposure suspected, without one established infectious cause

rows.label: Clues
items: Dry cough, exertional dyspnea; restrictive physiology and ↓DLCO; upper-lung interstitial infiltrates
★ **Löfgren syndrome**: erythema nodosum + ankle arthritis + hilar adenopathy; usually favorable prognosis
Uveitis, lupus pernio, parotid enlargement; facial palsy, hypothalamic dysfunction suggest neurosarcoidosis
★ Unexplained **AV block, ventricular arrhythmia, syncope** → cardiac involvement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CD4-mediated granulomas; macrophage 1α-hydroxylase → ↑calcitriol, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria, suppressed PTH

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Chest radiograph**, PFTs; baseline calcium, creatinine, liver tests, ECG and eye examination
Compatible presentation + **noncaseating granulomas** + exclusion of TB/fungi/beryllium exposure
Sample accessible lesion or EBUS-guided hilar/mediastinal node; classic Löfgren presentation may avoid biopsy
ACE level neither sensitive nor specific; cardiac symptoms/ECG abnormalities → cardiac MRI ± FDG-PET

rows.label: Tx
items: Asymptomatic stage I disease, preserved function → observation with clinical/PFT follow-up
★ **Prednisone** for progressive symptomatic pulmonary disease, significant hypercalcemia, cardiac or neurologic disease
Uveitis → urgent ophthalmology, topical or systemic corticosteroids according to severity
Steroid-dependent disease → methotrexate; refractory organ-threatening disease → specialist-directed infliximab
Hypercalcemia → hydration; restrict excess calcium/vitamin D and sunlight exposure

rows.label: Complications
items: Pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary hypertension, respiratory failure; nephrolithiasis and kidney injury
Cardiomyopathy, sudden death; visual loss; chronic steroids → infection, osteoporosis, diabetes

rows.label: Prevention
items: No established primary prevention; smoking cessation and vaccination reduce respiratory morbidity
Monitor treatment toxicity and bone health; individualize vitamin D replacement because calcitriol may already be elevated

rows.label: Mimics
items: TB/fungal infection: organisms or positive microbiology; exclude before immunosuppression
Berylliosis: aerospace/industrial exposure, positive beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test
Lymphoma: malignant tissue, constitutional symptoms; granulomas alone do not exclude concurrent cancer

secondary-hypertension.name: Secondary hypertension
secondary-hypertension.scope: Renal artery stenosis, primary hyperaldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation of aorta, diagnostic workup
secondary-hypertension.core: Abrupt, unusually young, severe, or resistant hypertension suggests a treatable secondary driver.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Atherosclerosis, fibromuscular dysplasia, renal disease, adrenal tumors, sleep apnea
NSAIDs, oral contraceptives, stimulants, glucocorticoids, licorice; medication nonadherence can mimic resistance

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Hypokalemia** suggests mineralocorticoid excess but normal K does not exclude it
Flash pulmonary edema or creatinine rise >30% after ACE inhibitor/ARB → renovascular disease
Endocrine spells, cushingoid appearance, or upper-body hypertension guide cause-specific testing

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Renal hypoperfusion activates RAAS; mineralocorticoid signaling increases distal sodium absorption and potassium loss
Catecholamine/cortisol excess, aortic obstruction, or nocturnal hypoxia increases vascular pressure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Confirm **home/ambulatory BP**, adherence, cuff technique; BMP, urinalysis, creatinine, TSH
Sleep-apnea symptoms → polysomnography; abnormal urinary sediment → renal ultrasound and kidney evaluation
★ Biochemical testing precedes adrenal imaging; correct hypokalemia and account for interfering medications
Endocrine Society 2025: suggest **aldosterone screening for all hypertension**, conditional on resources

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Primary aldosteronism: unilateral → **adrenalectomy**; bilateral → spironolactone/eplerenone
Renovascular atherosclerosis → medical risk reduction; revascularize selected recurrent pulmonary edema or refractory disease
Fibromuscular dysplasia → angioplasty; critical bilateral renal stenosis → avoid ACE inhibitor/ARB
★ Pheochromocytoma: **alpha blockade before beta blockade**, volume expansion, then surgery
Treat cortisol source, repair significant coarctation, use CPAP for OSA; stop contributing drugs

rows.label: Complications
items: Stroke, MI, heart failure, CKD, retinopathy
Unopposed alpha stimulation after beta blockade can cause catecholamine crisis

rows.label: Prevention
items: Monitor renal function/K after RAAS blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists
Genetic evaluation/family screening for suspected hereditary pheochromocytoma or congenital aortic disease

rows.label: Mimics
items: White-coat hypertension: normal out-of-office readings
Essential hypertension: gradual course without specific endocrine/renal clues

table.title: Targeted workup
rows: Selective suppression test; CT/adrenal venous sampling
Plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines

secondary-hypertension.evidence: Aldosterone screening checked 2026-10-30: [Endocrine Society 2025](https://www.endocrine.org/clinical-practice-guidelines/primary-aldosteronism-2); other causes: established teaching.

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.name: Skin and soft tissue infections
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.scope: Cellulitis, erysipelas, folliculitis, furuncles, carbuncles, lymphangitis, necrotizing fasciitis
skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.core: Skin infection management depends on purulence, systemic illness, and signs of deep tissue destruction.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Skin breaks, tinea pedis, edema/lymphedema, diabetes, obesity, injection drug use
Prior MRSA, crowding, recent hospitalization; surgery or penetrating trauma raises deep-infection risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Warmth, tenderness, erythema; rapidly expanding margins or systemic toxicity require urgent reassessment
★ **Pain out of proportion**, bullae, anesthesia, crepitus, shock → necrotizing infection
Perineal involvement → Fournier gangrene; saltwater exposure → Vibrio, freshwater → Aeromonas

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Nonpurulent infection usually streptococcal; purulent lesions usually S aureus
Fascial spread and toxin-mediated injury → thrombosis, necrosis, sepsis

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Clinical diagnosis; **bedside ultrasound** if occult fluid collection suspected
Culture drained pus for severe, recurrent, or resistant infection; blood cultures for systemic toxicity
Suspected necrotizing disease → immediate surgical evaluation; imaging must not delay exploration
Low laboratory risk score or absent gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Deep infection → **urgent debridement + vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam**, add clindamycin for toxin suppression
Confirmed group A streptococcal necrotizing infection → penicillin + clindamycin
Severe cellulitis/systemic illness → IV cefazolin; MRSA risk → vancomycin
★ Abscess: add **antibiotics** for systemic signs, immunocompromise, extensive disease, or failed drainage

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, osteomyelitis, septic thrombophlebitis; tissue loss and amputation
Toxic shock, multiorgan failure; recurrent cellulitis worsens lymphatic dysfunction

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat interdigital fungal infection, manage edema, skin hygiene, protect wounds
Recurrent staphylococcal infections → consider nasal mupirocin + chlorhexidine decolonization; avoid shared razors

rows.label: Mimics
items: Stasis dermatitis: chronic, often bilateral, itchy
DVT: deep swelling without superficial spreading infection; contact dermatitis: pruritic exposure-pattern rash

table.title: Superficial patterns
rows: Incision and drainage; TMP-SMX if needed

skin-and-soft-tissue-infections.evidence: Not checked online; established IDSA-based infection management.

spinal-cord-injury.name: Spinal cord injury
spinal-cord-injury.scope: Traumatic spinal cord injury, incomplete cord syndromes, neurogenic shock, dermatome mapping, vertebral level
spinal-cord-injury.core: Trauma with weakness, a sensory level, and sphincter dysfunction demands spinal protection and urgent imaging; neurologic level may differ from vertebral injury.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Motor vehicle collision, falls, diving, penetrating injury; cervical stenosis predisposes to hyperextension injury

rows.label: Clues
items: Acute spinal shock: flaccid areflexia below lesion; later spasticity/hyperreflexia; assess sacral sparing
★ **Neurogenic shock**: hypotension, bradycardia, warm skin after high cord injury; exclude hemorrhage first
C3–5 involvement threatens diaphragmatic function; priapism and urinary retention support cord disruption

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Primary cord damage + secondary edema/ischemia; sympathetic interruption causes vasodilation and unopposed vagal tone

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ ABCs with **cervical immobilization** → CT spine for fracture; persistent neurologic deficits → **MRI**
Document motor/sensory level, rectal tone, perianal sensation; S4–5 sparing defines incomplete injury
Dermatomes: C6 thumb, C7 middle finger, C8 little finger, T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus, S4–5 perianal
Motor: C5 elbow flexion, C6 wrist extension, C7 elbow extension, C8 finger flexion, T1 finger abduction
Cord ends around L1–2 vertebrae; lower vertebral injuries may damage nerve roots rather than cord

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Support ventilation, avoid hypoxia/hypotension; hemorrhage → blood; neurogenic shock → cautious fluids, **norepinephrine**
Urgent decompression/stabilization for compressive or unstable injuries; early specialist transfer
★ **No routine high-dose methylprednisolone**; infection/bleeding harms outweigh established benefit
Rehabilitation, pressure relief, intermittent catheterization, bowel regimen, VTE prophylaxis
Autonomic dysreflexia → sit upright, loosen clothing, empty bladder; persistent severe hypertension → topical nitroglycerin

rows.label: Complications
items: Autonomic dysreflexia after injury ≥T6: bladder/bowel trigger → severe hypertension, headache, sweating above lesion
Pressure injuries, DVT/PE, recurrent UTI, respiratory failure, contractures, chronic neuropathic pain

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seatbelts, helmets, fall prevention, safe diving; maintain skin checks and bladder/bowel schedules

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cauda equina: asymmetric radicular pain, saddle anesthesia, LMN weakness, reduced reflexes
Guillain-Barré: ascending areflexia without discrete sensory level; often preceding infection

table.title: Incomplete cord syndromes
rows: Ipsilateral motor/vibration; contralateral pain/temperature starts 1–2 levels below

spinal-cord-injury.evidence: Autonomic dysreflexia checked 2026-10-30: [PVA clinician guideline](https://pva.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/cpg_autonomic-dysreflexia.pdf); remaining acute management: established trauma teaching.

subarachnoid-hemorrhage.name: Subarachnoid hemorrhage
subarachnoid-hemorrhage.scope: Ruptured saccular aneurysm, thunderclap headache, noncontrast head CT, lumbar puncture and xanthochromia, nimodipine, complications
subarachnoid-hemorrhage.core: Sudden headache maximal within seconds, often during exertion, with possible meningismus or collapse: presume subarachnoid hemorrhage until excluded.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, hypertension, family history, prior aneurysm; autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Ruptured saccular aneurysm usually near circle-of-Willis branch points; cocaine increases rupture risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Vomiting, photophobia, neck stiffness, transient loss of consciousness; sentinel headache may precede major hemorrhage
★ **Painful pupil-involving CN III palsy** → posterior communicating artery aneurysm
Declining consciousness, focal deficits or seizures → high-risk presentation; normal examination does not exclude hemorrhage

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Blood enters subarachnoid space → meningeal irritation, ↑ICP, impaired CSF resorption
Blood-breakdown products and vascular injury contribute to delayed cerebral ischemia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Noncontrast head CT immediately**; sensitivity declines with elapsed time
★ Negative CT >6 hours after onset or neurologic deficit → **LP**, assessing xanthochromia and RBCs
High-quality CT within 6 hours, neurologically intact, expert interpretation → may exclude SAH without routine LP
Confirmed blood → **CT angiography**; negative/inconclusive CTA with suspected aneurysm → catheter angiography
Traumatic tap may show falling RBCs; clearing alone cannot reliably exclude SAH

rows.label: Tx
items: Support airway, reverse anticoagulation, analgesia; severe hypertension → IV nicardipine; avoid hypotension/BP swings
★ **Urgent aneurysm coiling or clipping**, preferably within 24 hours, prevents rebleeding
★ **Enteral nimodipine for 21 days**, maintain euvolemia; no prophylactic hypervolemia
Acute symptomatic hydrocephalus → external ventricular drainage
Secured aneurysm + delayed ischemia → induced hypertension; refractory → endovascular vasodilator/angioplasty

rows.label: Complications
items: Early rebleeding, hydrocephalus, seizures; delayed ischemia typically days 3–14
Hyponatremia from SIADH or cerebral salt wasting; stress cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, pulmonary edema

rows.label: Prevention
items: Smoking cessation and BP control; specialist screening discussion for ≥2 affected first-degree relatives or high-risk ADPKD

rows.label: Mimics
items: Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction: recurrent thunderclap headaches; segmental angiographic narrowing
Meningitis: fever and inflammatory CSF rather than aneurysmal bleeding
Migraine: usually slower onset, recurrent stereotyped episodes; first thunderclap still needs hemorrhage evaluation

syphilis.name: Syphilis
syphilis.scope: Primary syphilis, secondary syphilis, latent syphilis, tertiary syphilis, neurosyphilis, serologic testing, Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, penicillin therapy
syphilis.core: Treponema pallidum infection progresses through mucocutaneous, asymptomatic, and destructive stages; neurologic, ocular, or auditory disease can occur anytime.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unprotected sex, multiple partners, HIV; transplacental transmission during pregnancy

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Primary: **painless chancre** with regional lymphadenopathy
Secondary: palms/soles rash, condylomata lata, generalized nodes, patchy alopecia
Tertiary: gummas, ascending aortic aneurysm; tabes dorsalis or dementia
Latent: reactive serology without symptoms; early = acquired within 1 year

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Spirochete dissemination → endarteritis; posterior column injury → sensory ataxia

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RPR/VDRL + treponemal assay**; discordant reverse screen → second treponemal assay
Early chancre with negative serology → lesion testing or repeat serology
★ Neurologic deficits → **LP**; CSF-VDRL specific, negative result does not exclude
Quantitative RPR: early disease follow-up at 6/12 months; latent at 6/12/24 months
Tertiary disease → CSF assessment before treatment; isolated ocular/otic disease may not require LP

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Pregnancy with penicillin allergy → **desensitization**, then stage-specific penicillin
Nonpregnant penicillin allergy, uncomplicated early infection → doxycycline for 14 days

rows.label: Complications
items: Jarisch-Herxheimer: fever/myalgias within 24 hours after treatment; supportive care, not allergy
Congenital infection → stillbirth, hearing loss, dental/bone abnormalities

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Partners exposed within **90 days** → presumptive early-syphilis treatment despite negative tests
HIV testing; prenatal screening; serial RPR after treatment, fourfold rise suggests reinfection/failure

rows.label: Mimics
items: Chancroid: painful ulcer, tender suppurative nodes
HSV: painful grouped vesicles; pityriasis rosea: herald patch, usually spares palms
Autoimmune false-positive RPR: negative confirmatory treponemal assay

syphilis.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [CDC STI guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/std/treatment-guidelines/syphilis.htm), including linked stage-specific guidance.

thoracic-trauma.name: Thoracic trauma
thoracic-trauma.scope: Blunt and penetrating chest trauma, blunt cardiac injury, blunt aortic injury, diaphragmatic rupture, pulmonary contusion
thoracic-trauma.core: Chest trauma with respiratory or circulatory compromise requires immediate treatment of life-threatening injuries before definitive imaging.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, steering-wheel impact, crush injuries, penetrating wounds
Lower chest wounds can cross diaphragm and injure abdominal organs

rows.label: Clues
items: Unilateral absent breath sounds, shock, distended neck veins → tension pneumothorax
Flail segment: paradoxical movement; associated lung injury drives hypoxemia
Delayed respiratory deterioration after blunt impact → pulmonary contusion
Left thoracic bowel sounds or elevated hemidiaphragm → diaphragmatic rupture

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Pleural pressure or pericardial blood impairs venous return → obstructive shock
Alveolar hemorrhage and edema impair gas exchange; rapid deceleration shears the aortic isthmus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Primary survey with **eFAST** and portable chest radiograph; unstable injuries treated clinically
★ Suspected aortic injury, stable → **CT angiography**; normal radiograph cannot exclude
Blunt cardiac injury → ECG and troponin; both normal effectively exclude significant injury
New arrhythmia or elevated troponin → telemetry; persistent shock → echocardiography

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Tension pneumothorax → immediate needle/finger decompression → **chest tube**; no imaging delay
Open pneumothorax → vented seal and tube; hemothorax → tube and blood resuscitation
★ Initial tube blood >1500 mL or persistent >200 mL/h → operative exploration
Tamponade with shock/arrest → surgical drainage; pericardiocentesis only temporizing
Contusion/flail chest → oxygen, regional/multimodal analgesia, pulmonary hygiene; intubate for respiratory failure

rows.label: Complications
items: Contusion → ARDS; retained hemothorax → empyema
Rib fractures → splinting, atelectasis, pneumonia; cardiac injury → arrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Seat belts, vehicle safety systems and protective equipment reduce injury risk

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiogenic shock: ventricular dysfunction without pericardial compression
Abdominal hemorrhage: free intraperitoneal fluid; may coexist with thoracic injury

thoracic-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established ATLS-based teaching.

table.title: Definitive associated-injury management
rows: IV esmolol if tolerated; endovascular repair

transfusion-reactions.name: Transfusion reactions
transfusion-reactions.scope: Acute hemolytic, febrile nonhemolytic, TRALI, TACO, anaphylactic, delayed hemolytic, massive transfusion complications
transfusion-reactions.core: New symptoms during transfusion require stopping the transfusion immediately and evaluating hemolysis, infection and cardiopulmonary compromise.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior transfusion/pregnancy → alloantibodies; IgA deficiency with anti-IgA → anaphylaxis
Heart/kidney failure, rapid infusion, older age → circulatory overload

rows.label: Clues
items: Delayed hemolysis: hemoglobin falls with jaundice days–weeks after apparently compatible transfusion
Bacterial contamination: high fever, rigors, profound hypotension; platelets particularly vulnerable
Isolated urticaria without systemic symptoms suggests mild allergic reaction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: ABO mismatch → complement-mediated intravascular lysis; anamnestic antibodies → delayed extravascular hemolysis
TRALI: inflammatory pulmonary capillary leak; TACO: hydrostatic pressure from excess circulating volume

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Keep IV access with saline; **recheck patient/unit identity**, notify blood bank
Hemolysis workup: DAT, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, plasma/urine hemoglobin; send unit and blood samples
Fever/shock → patient and product cultures; dyspnea → chest radiograph, oxygenation, volume assessment
Suspected febrile nonhemolytic reaction remains diagnosis of exclusion after hemolysis/sepsis evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Acute hemolysis → IV saline, support renal perfusion, treat shock/DIC; **never restart unit**
★ Anaphylaxis → **IM epinephrine**, airway support; future washed or IgA-deficient products
TRALI → supportive oxygen/ventilation; diuretics generally unhelpful unless concomitant overload
TACO → upright positioning, oxygen, **IV furosemide**; slow future transfusions
Suspected contamination → broad IV antibiotics; mild isolated allergy → diphenhydramine after clinical reassessment

rows.label: Complications
items: Acute hemolysis → AKI, DIC; severe pulmonary reactions → respiratory failure
Massive transfusion → citrate hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, hypothermia, dilutional thrombocytopenia/coagulopathy

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Bedside identification and crossmatch; leukoreduction reduces febrile reactions
Massive hemorrhage → balanced blood components, temperature and ionized calcium monitoring

rows.label: Mimics
items: Underlying sepsis: symptoms may precede infusion; cultures clarify
Aspiration: event-linked infiltrate without transfusion-specific mechanism

transfusion-reactions.evidence: Not checked online; established transfusion-medicine definitions.

tuberculosis.name: Tuberculosis
tuberculosis.scope: Latent TB infection screening (PPD, IGRA), treatment regimens, active pulmonary TB, acid-fast bacilli smear and culture, RIPE therapy, extrapulmonary TB (Pott disease)
tuberculosis.core: Chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, and upper-lobe cavitation suggest contagious pulmonary tuberculosis; latent infection has no active disease.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Close contact, endemic-area residence, incarceration, homelessness, crowded housing
HIV, TNF inhibitors, transplant, silicosis, diabetes → progression/reactivation risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Hemoptysis, prolonged fever; primary disease may cause hilar adenopathy or pleural effusion
★ **Back pain with vertebral destruction** → Pott disease; miliary spread causes diffuse micronodules

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Airborne bacilli survive in macrophages; cell-mediated granulomas contain infection until immune failure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Screening: **IGRA** preferred after BCG; TST read induration at 48–72 hours
Positive screening → symptoms + chest radiograph; neither test distinguishes latent from active infection
★ Active suspicion → **sputum NAAT, AFB smear, culture and susceptibility**; collect serial specimens
Negative smear or IGRA does not exclude active TB, especially with immunosuppression
Pott suspicion → spinal MRI, biopsy/culture; assess cord compression

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Suspected contagious disease → **airborne isolation** and public-health notification
Drug-susceptible active TB: 2 months isoniazid/rifampin/pyrazinamide/ethambutol → 4 months isoniazid/rifampin
Eligible pulmonary cases ≥12 years: 4-month isoniazid/rifapentine/moxifloxacin/pyrazinamide-based regimen alternative
Latent: prefer 3-month weekly isoniazid/rifapentine or 4-month rifampin; exclude active disease first
Isoniazid → pyridoxine for neuropathy risk; Pott with neurologic deficit/instability → urgent spinal surgical evaluation

rows.label: Complications
items: Meningitis, adrenal destruction, spinal cord compression, bronchiectasis
INH/rifampin/pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity; ethambutol: optic neuropathy; rifampin: enzyme induction, orange secretions

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Contact investigation**, latent-treatment completion; directly observed active treatment improves adherence
Review drug interactions and baseline liver risk; monitor visual acuity/color vision with ethambutol

rows.label: Mimics
items: Lung cancer: focal malignant biopsy
Fungal infection: geographic exposure; nontuberculous mycobacteria: species identification distinguishes

table.title: Positive TST thresholds
rows: HIV, close contacts, transplant, substantial immunosuppression
Exposure-risk groups, comorbidity risks, young children

urinary-incontinence.name: Urinary incontinence
urinary-incontinence.core: Involuntary urine leakage is classified by triggers, urgency, bladder emptying, and ability to reach a toilet; reversible contributors often coexist.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Childbirth, pelvic surgery, aging, obesity; diabetes, neurologic disease, prostate enlargement
Diuretics, sedatives, anticholinergics, constipation, infection, impaired mobility/cognition worsen control

rows.label: Clues
items: History: timing, volume, dysuria, weak stream, nocturia, fluid intake, obstetric/surgical and neurologic history
★ **New saddle anesthesia, leg weakness, retention** → urgent cauda equina evaluation
Continuous leakage after pelvic surgery suggests fistula; recurrent UTIs/hematuria require further investigation

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Urethral support/sphincter failure, involuntary detrusor contraction, or impaired emptying produce distinct leakage patterns
Functional impairment can prevent continence despite intact lower urinary tract function

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis + voiding diary**, focused pelvic/prostate and neurologic examination; review medications
Cough stress test with reasonably full bladder; assess prolapse, atrophy, fecal impaction
★ Suspected retention/emptying symptoms → **postvoid residual**; persistent >200 mL suggests inadequate emptying
No routine initial urodynamics/cystoscopy; uncertainty, hematuria, refractory symptoms → additional testing

rows.label: Tx
items: Treat reversible contributor; mixed incontinence → target most bothersome component
★ **Pelvic floor training/bladder training** underpin conservative care; weight loss, reduce caffeine, timed voiding
Urgency drugs: mirabegron or antimuscarinic; discuss cognitive risk and avoid antimuscarinics with retention
Mirabegron may increase BP; avoid severe uncontrolled hypertension; refractory urgency → botulinum toxin or neuromodulation
Genitourinary syndrome of menopause → local vaginal estrogen when suitable; not systemic estrogen for leakage

rows.label: Complications
items: Dermatitis, falls from rushing, social isolation, sleep disruption
Overflow → hydronephrosis/renal injury; bladder botulinum toxin → retention, UTI

rows.label: Prevention
items: Medication review, accessible toilet, mobility aids; bowel regularity, maintain strength and weight

rows.label: Mimics
items: Polyuria: high urine volume from hyperglycemia/diuresis rather than primary storage failure
Vaginal fistula: constant leakage unrelated to voiding urge or exertion

urinary-tract-infections.name: Urinary tract infections
urinary-tract-infections.scope: Asymptomatic bacteriuria, acute cystitis, pyelonephritis, catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), catheter removal, empiric antibiotics
urinary-tract-infections.core: Symptoms localize urinary infection: bladder disease lacks systemic illness; renal involvement causes fever or flank pain; bacteriuria alone is insufficient.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Sexual activity, spermicides, pregnancy, obstruction/stones, urinary retention, instrumentation
Catheter duration, diabetes, prior resistant isolates or antibiotics increase complicated-course risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic discomfort; absent vaginal discharge supports urinary source
★ **Rigors, CVA tenderness, vomiting, hypotension** → pyelonephritis or urosepsis
Catheterized patients: new urinary/systemic symptoms; cloudy urine or pyuria alone insufficient

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Usually ascending enteric bacteria, predominantly E coli; catheter biofilm maintains colonization
Urease-producing Proteus alkalinizes urine → struvite calculi and persistent infection

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Urinalysis**: pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites; negative nitrites do not exclude infection
Culture: pyelonephritis, pregnancy, CAUTI, recurrence/resistance; classic cystitis often clinical
Persistent fever after 48–72 hours, sepsis, or suspected obstruction → renal imaging
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: usually ≥100,000 CFU/mL; delirium alone → seek other causes without automatic antibiotics

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria only in pregnancy or before urologic mucosal trauma** in routine adult scenarios
★ CAUTI → **remove unnecessary catheter**; if needed and present >2 weeks, replace before culture/treatment
★ Infected obstructed collecting system → **urgent drainage + IV antibiotics**; antibiotics alone insufficient
Improving nonpregnant pyelonephritis: fluoroquinolone 5–7 days, other active drugs 7 days; high-risk cases individualized

rows.label: Complications
items: Bacteremia, septic shock, renal/perinephric abscess; pregnancy → preterm birth
Antibiotics → resistance, C difficile; fluoroquinolones → tendon injury, QT prolongation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid unnecessary catheters; closed drainage, daily removal assessment
Postmenopausal recurrence → vaginal estrogen; selected recurrences → postcoital/continuous antibiotic prophylaxis

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vaginitis: discharge, pruritus, external burning
Urethritis: sexual exposure, discharge, positive gonorrhea/chlamydia NAAT
Bladder pain syndrome: chronic symptoms, repeatedly negative cultures

table.title: Initial antibiotics; tailor to culture/resistance
rows: Ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin; initial ceftriaxone if resistance risk
IV ceftriaxone; cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam if Pseudomonas risk
Avoid nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin: inadequate renal tissue levels
